paragraphs.text: The lesson, then, is not "start the highest-risk port first" but something narrower and harder: start the highest-risk piece early enough to rehearse with it. A port can land on time and still be the piece most likely to change in the last hour, because the person who will stand on stage with it has not yet used it. Chapter 8 shows what that last hour cost: the session taking the editor's player notes at 18:25 was the session that was meant to lock the first part of the talk at 18:30.

The player was not written. It was copied from ruv.sgit.ai's talk player, from a repository in the same organisation under the Apache-2.0 licence, with its notice kept and nothing loaded from ruv.sgit.ai when it runs ( team/dev/debriefs/2026-10-29__the-player.md ). Dev's brief for the port, written from the editor's words at about 14:50, lists what it kept feature by feature: play and pause, slides and steps forward and back, two stops for every step (its beginning and its built end, so going back never lands on a blank frame), the countdown, the talk timer, presenter notes, the audience window, the rehearsal log. The editor called the two-stops idea "quite an important concept", and it came from his own note of 15 October, already built into the player he was porting.

What dev added was small and decisive. The player now counted down the time the editor said he had, not the talk's planned length. It knew the talk's acts as sections. And it made every piece of the studio playable as a slide, because this site's slide engine answered the ported player's clock contract itself: any page that declared its steps could be paused, sped up, scrubbed and stepped by the player, and stepping back needed no reload. That one adapter is why the afternoon could move so fast. Every member who made a moving piece, ruv-sgit with its experiments, the new studio with its ports, motion with the new story's animations, made it for the same clock, so deck could put any of them on a beat without asking dev for anything.
The ported player, afternoon of 29 October 2026: overview, presenting, on an iPad, and the editor's feedback pane

The port also shows a control working in the middle of the rush. Dev's pre-review asked for the player's offline cache to be dropped: a service worker at the site's root caches every member's pages, and no member owned that file. The port went out without it. At 15:35 the cache came back with the editor's own grant recorded in dev's policy, in his words ( 588b11a ). The scope rule did not stop the feature; it made the person who could grant the reach grant it, in writing, before it shipped.

The studio member was the same idea given a role. Its mandate was ports and adaptations of ruv.sgit.ai's pieces onto this site's engine, each keeping its notice, each saying where it came from and what changed, each tracing every number on screen to its source or to the claims register ( team/studio/ROLE.md ). The editor had asked that ruv.sgit.ai's animations be reviewed and reused before new ones were made, and the team answered with a member whose whole job was reuse.
Studio's ports of ruv.sgit.ai pieces onto the site's engine, late afternoon, one of them playing in the player

There is an argument here worth making plainly. The talk's own beat on explorer coding ( spreadsheets ) says that people who once built a spreadsheet now build an application with a coding agent in an afternoon, and that every one of those applications starts its security from nothing. This team is a case of the first half and a counter-example to the second. Its applications, the player, the lock tool, the lane, the build mode, were built in an afternoon. But none of them started from nothing: they started from a port with a known licence, inside a repository whose gate had run since the first commit, in a scope a pre-review read before any line was written. The explosion of software is real. What decides whether it is dangerous is what each new application inherits.

Three members joined in the afternoon (C011). The storyteller's first wake started at 14:12 and its join commit landed at 14:15 (C012). Motion and studio joined together at 15:31 ( f1cbca0 , 8d208d3 , C013), soon after the conductor wrote their briefs and first prompts at 15:25 ( f00734f ). Each arrived with a role, a policy, a session key and its own scheduled task, and each closed its first wake within minutes; studio ported its first pieces in that wake. At 15:47 the conductor checked both new keys and routed their first requests ( 4adc04a ). Studio's third port landed at 16:18 ( 0fe0fff ), and motion's first piece, the building, where attackers turn left towards small things and agents turn right towards the gold, was on the engine with its stops at 16:34 ( 7639664 ).

paragraphs.text: Joining in one wake was possible because of everything chapters 3 and 4 describe. The mandate had a template, the key had a pinned tool, the wake had five steps and a record, the schedule had a free slot, and the conductor had a way to check a newcomer. None of it was built for the afternoon; all of it was built in the first hours of the night and used, from then on, without anyone re-deciding it. A team that has to design its onboarding while it onboards cannot add a member an hour before a deadline. This one added two in the same minute.

Motion's role says why the team took a second animator rather than asking ruv-sgit for more: "so neither member waits on the other and no file has two owners" ( team/motion/ROLE.md ). That sentence is the afternoon's method in small. Speed came from splitting ownership finely enough that nobody's work blocked anybody else's: deck owned what the talk said, dev owned the engine and the player, ruv-sgit the studio programme, studio the ports, motion the new animations, the storyteller the arc, the researcher the facts. When a beat needed a change in someone else's file it became a request, not an edit. The member count matters less than the boundaries between them.

The cost of joining fast is in the commit counts. By the end of the day studio had 26 commits naming it and motion 9 (C014), against ruv-sgit's 84 and dev's 64. Members who join at half past three have an evening, not a day. The pieces they made were for the talk's later parts, and chapter 8 shows that the later parts were the ones still in progress when the team stopped.

paragraphs.text: At 16:32 the conductor routed the editor's word that the talk was ninety minutes long, with a section on the editor's own work ( 62c6b99 ). At 16:36 deck set the talk in the editor's order, and it had twenty-two beats ( ca59986 ). At 17:09 deck interleaved the studio's pieces and the talk had thirty-eight ( 7f522de ). At 17:52 deck marked part 1 final for its lock and the talk had fifty-eight ( b1c9bab , C016). The talk that had stood at seventeen beats since the first hour more than tripled between 16:36 and 17:52.
Deck's new slides as it set the talk in the editor's order (29 October 2026, 16:36)

The fifty-eight beats fell into three parts: twenty-two in the first, sixteen in the second, twenty in the third (C015). Most of the growth was not new writing. It was the night's and the afternoon's pieces, already built on the shared clock, being placed: experiments from the studio programme, ports from studio, motion's animations, and live slides that opened the team's own tools on stage. The pieces existed; the talk caught up with them.

One part of that catching up went out of order. The editor's plan of about 17:00 asked the storyteller to split the arc into three parts and send the split to deck by 17:30. Deck did not wait. It set part 1 itself, complete and timed, at 17:25 ( 3260997 ). The storyteller's split arrived at 17:51 and says so in its first lines: "Deck set part 1 itself without waiting for this split, which was due at 17:30 and is late. So part 1 gets notes only, and parts 2 and 3 get the placement" ( team/storyteller/story/three-parts.md , 14998b5 ). Neither member is at fault in a useful sense. The storyteller had joined at 14:15, and deck had a deadline that would not move. But the sequence the team had built its method on, nothing enters the talk until the storyteller has mapped it (chapter 5), was reversed for the part the audience would hear first. The storyteller's notes on part 1 were offered "take them or leave them", and at its 18:14 check it set part 1 aside entirely, as locked or locking, and found named gaps in parts 2 and 3 instead ( team/storyteller/story/part-check-1814.md ).

The growth in beats hides a change in what the talk was. The first pass was a talk about agents as the ultimate insider, illustrated. By 17:52 it was also a demonstration of an agent team, given by the person who ran it, while it was still running.

The editor's words in the conductor's session between 17:16 and 17:48 drove most of that change, and they arrived as fast as the conductor could route them: answers on the live slides, "when in doubt add it", the team's own policies into the talk, "go build", how the team keeps itself safe ( team/conductor/briefs/2026-10-29__editor/ , briefs 6 to 10). Deck added a set of live slides at 17:21, pages that opened running software on stage rather than pictures of it ( ef05098 , da9b681 ). The researcher catalogued the editor's own work for the showcase slides and checked every crop for keys before it shipped ( 7bda718 , a867f7f ). The team's own behaviour policies, the ones chapter 3 describes, became a beat of part 2, and the storyteller's split asked that it be said honestly: "a scope is a setting, not a boundary" ( three-parts.md , part 2, item 8). The designer checked part 1 on a projector at 17:48 and found it ready ( ec962a2 ).

This matters for the book's argument because it changed the stakes of the making. A talk that shows the team's policies, keys and wake records as evidence is a talk whose evidence is the repository itself. Every shortcut the team took that evening was, in principle, on stage. The beat's own cue said what kept that safe: "Benign only: nothing attack-shaped about the team. The site's agents page is the evidence" ( talk.json , beat team ). The team that built the talk was asked to be its exhibit, and the exhibit had to hold up to an audience that could read it live. That is a stronger test of a method than any review step, and it is the reason this book can be written from the record at all.

It also explains why the talk grew in the way it did. Most of what joined it after 16:36 was not argument but demonstration: the studio's pieces, the ports, the live tools, the team's own pages. The editor's plan of about 17:00 said it directly: "what's going to be powerful is to even show some of our workflows happening ... in action", with the team still changing the later parts while he presented the first ( 3-three-parts-and-locks-1700.md ). Chapter 8 follows that plan to its end.

One quieter cost of the afternoon's speed is in how the work is signed. From 01:40 the house form was a commit subject that opened with the member's name, @dev: or @deck: , and a trailer naming the agent. In the evening that form slipped. The player's commits from 16:36 onwards open with "Player:", the lock tool with "Locked parts:", and a style fix in ruv-sgit's pieces with the pieces' own names. A count of commits by subject alone leaves them unattributed, and the timeline does the same; the register, which reads their trailers too, gives them to dev (C014).

paragraphs.text: Read in full, these commits are not anonymous: each carries an Agent: dev@the-ultimate-insider trailer and dev's session link. The record knows whose they are; the form the team had agreed for reading it at a glance did not survive the evening. That is a small thing, and it is also the pattern of the evening in chapter 8: a rule that held while the team had time to follow it, bending at exactly the point where the editor's notes arrived faster than the house style could carry them.

The talk's turn from part one to part two was a beat called team , written for the editor to say about the people (and agents) who made the talk he was giving. Each member has a role, a mandate, a scope it may write, its own key, an hourly wake, and a review before and after every wake; "the capability is the orchestration, not the model." The making of the talk is the evidence for that line, and it is worth being precise about what the evidence shows.
![The team beat, 'This site is made by a team of agents' (still shot after the day from v0.2.0, whose content is the 18:46 release)](../../book/resources/images/07-team-slide.jpg)

It does not show that any single agent was remarkable. The player was a port; the ports were copies with notices; the beats were mostly placements of pieces already built. What it shows is that a team organised around ownership, a shared clock and a written record could absorb a ninety-minute talk, three new members, a ported player and a new structure between the editor's briefs at 14:07 and the player's last fix at 18:37, with the editor speaking and the team doing. That is the explosion of software the talk warns about, seen from the inside: one person, without writing code, had a player ported, a build mode made, a feedback lane built, a lock tool written and a talk tripled, by asking.

It also shows where that kind of speed breaks. Work that waits on one person piles up while he is away, and is cleared only when he returns. The highest-risk piece is not the hardest to build but the one the person on stage has not yet used, and it changes last. A sequence the method depends on (map, then write) is the first thing a deadline reverses. And the house forms that make a record readable at a glance slip before the record itself does. None of these is a reason not to build this way. Each is a reason to know, before the afternoon starts, which piece the editor must rehearse with, who owns the map when the deadline overruns it, and which control will hold the line when the notes come faster than the hour. The next chapter is about the one the team built for that last purpose, and why it never closed.

paragraphs.text: This chapter is about that collision. The talk's closing beat says "We put brakes in cars so that we can go faster", and the team spent its evening proving the first half of the sentence. It built a brake against its own last-minute changes, loosened another so it could move faster, kept the five steps and the gate in place under the most pressure of the day, and was finally stopped by a brake nobody on the team controlled. Two brakes met at the end of the day, and the stronger one stopped the other. The argument of this chapter is that the right one won, and that the reason it won is the most useful thing the day has to teach about brakes.

The afternoon's last structural change began at 16:32, when the conductor routed the editor's word that the talk was ninety minutes long and would include a section on his own work ( 62c6b99 ). The talk then had seventeen beats (C016). A ninety-minute talk needed a structure the team could finish in pieces, and the editor gave it one at about 16:55. His words, as the conductor recorded them, are worth reading for what they ask of the team:

"break the presentation into three parts ... you guys can still be making changes to the second part while I present ... as long as we don't break anything too badly ... we should be locking down a presentation and then not making any more changes to it" ( team/conductor/briefs/2026-10-29__editor/3-three-parts-and-locks-1700.md )

The conductor turned that into a table. Part 1 on stage from 19:00 and locked at 18:30; part 2 from 19:30 and locked at 19:30; part 3 from 20:00 and locked at 20:00. "Locked means locked": a locked part's files and version are never edited again, and work continues only in the next version, on the parts not yet locked. The editor reloads, and the player shows the latest version with the locked parts exactly as they were locked. Before every push from 18:30, a member checks that the locked parts still open and play.

Two things about the plan matter for what followed. The first is that it was a plan for change, not against it. The locks existed so that the team could keep changing the talk right up to and during the talk: each lock drew a line behind which the team could not reach, so that in front of it the team could go as fast as it liked. That is the talk's brakes argument applied to the talk itself. The second is that the plan's length did not yet match the slot. The beats, when they were all written, added up to 74.9 minutes, against the player's countdown of ninety (C026). Part 1 was 29.5 minutes, part 2 23.75, part 3 21.67 (C026). The first part was full; the second and third were still being filled when the day stopped.

The tool landed at 17:54 ( 4a2481b , C027). It is short, and it is a good piece of engineering for its purpose. admin/build/lock.py --part N opens every slide of the part from the built site in a browser, records every file each slide loads, copies those files into a locked folder that mirrors the site, writes the part's beats as they stand into that folder, and adds the part to a list of locks. The player, from the same commit, plays a locked part from its copy instead of from the live files. And the tool refuses to lock a part twice: "a locked part is never changed".

paragraphs.text: It was a brake in the strict sense the book uses: a setting, enforced by a tool, that refuses. Once part 1 was locked, the player would have played it from its frozen copy, so no member, however late its wake and however good its reason, could have changed what the editor saw in part 1; and the tool would have refused to lock it a second time. It protected the talk from the team, which in the last hour before a talk is the main thing a talk needs protecting from.

The commit says it was tried on part 1, every frozen file matching its live slide, and that the trial was then removed: "the real lock at 18:30". Its trailer names dev, and so do the files it touched (dev's policy and dev's wake record), though its subject, "Locked parts", names no member, which is why a count of commits by subject leaves it unattributed (C014). The tool existed, worked, and was ready before it was needed. Everything that went wrong with the locks went wrong after 17:54, and none of it was in the tool.

paragraphs.text: The commit that set the locks also relaxed the team's rhythm. Since 01:39 every member had woken once an hour, on the conductor's schedule, with a hold any member could pull ( 09f13d5 ). The editor asked for something faster: wakes more often than hourly until the talk. The platform refused. The conductor had tried a recurring task at that pace on its own schedule at 16:58 and been told no ( 3-three-parts-and-locks-1700.md , "The cadence until the talk"). That refusal is a small instance of the chapter's subject: a setting outside the team's reach, which the team did not try to get round. It designed within it instead. For tonight only, at the editor's word, a member with work left could end each wake by scheduling one one-off follow-up into its own session, and stop doing so when nothing was left, when another wake would add little, or at 20:00 London ( team/conductor/WAKE.md , the rule added in 3342cff ). Every follow-up was a full wake: the start script, the five steps, the gate, a pull before every push. A hold would stop it like any other wake.

This is turning point 7 in the timeline: the schedule relaxed ( timeline/turning-points.md ). It came after a step limit raised at 15:21 ( 545a473 ), when the work step that had been set short for a team running unattended at night was lengthened for a team racing a deadline with the editor in the room. Both changes made the team faster in the same way: they let a member keep working when the hourly rhythm would have made it stop.

What held, and what bent? The record is unusually clear. What held was the five steps. In the run of chat wakes the editor drove through the conductor's session between 17:16 and 17:48, the pre-review sent the conductor's plans back for change at 17:21, 17:30 and 17:45, and again at 18:19, each time before the work began, and each time the plan was amended and the wake went on (C023; the conductor's wake records, in their history ). The gate ran before every push. No step said stop all day (C023). The controls did not slow the editor's ideas down; they made each one pass a second reading first.

paragraphs.text: What bent was the rhythm the controls had been built around. Partial wakes clustered in the evening. Two wakes never closed: deck's at 18:20, which recorded only its plan, and dev's at 17:48, which recorded its plan and both reviews but no work or check (C022). And work began to land outside the house form, with subjects that named no member.

One detail of dev's unclosed wake matters more than the rest. Its plan, recorded at 17:50, covers the lock tool and the lock itself: "lock at 18:30, test open and play, no edits to locked/ after". The same plan ends "no send_later", reading dev's policy as not wanting it to schedule its own follow-ups ( team/dev/wakes/20261029T174850Z.json ; team/dev/policy.json , not_wanted ). The loosened rhythm, in other words, did not reach the member that held the lock. Dev would run when its hourly slot came round or when the editor opened a wake in its session. The relaxation that kept every other member going between slots did not apply to the one whose next action was the evening's most important brake.

The last hour can be told as a countdown. At 17:52 deck marked part 1 final for its lock ( b1c9bab ). At 17:54 the tool landed. At 18:01 the conductor's flag said part 1 was final and nothing would miss it ( 9d27703 ). At 18:14 deck put the title slide first, "before the 18:30 lock" ( b3f208f ); it was the last change to talk.json of the day. At 18:21 the conductor's flag said part 1 was ready for its lock ( 0ecddca ). At 18:30, the time the plan set, no lock ran. Motion closed a wake at 18:30:25 ( 5fd7877 ), but nothing ran lock.py , and there is no locked copy in the tree at the end of the day (C027).

At 18:36 the conductor checked, found part 1 still unlocked and unchanged since 18:30, and asked dev to run the lock now ( 2ed6427 , committed 18:39). In the same commit it told deck to treat part 1 as locked. That second instruction is worth pausing on. When the tool had not run, the conductor fell back on a rule: a member asked to behave as if a part were locked. A setting that refuses had become an expectation that a member is trusted to follow. Chapter 9 builds its whole register on that distinction. Here it appears in a single line of a commit message, at the moment the setting failed to arrive.
At 18:44 the hold came.

The hold is a short file, and the most important of the day. The conductor wrote it at 18:44:13 ( 867f8c2 , C006), at the editor's word in the conductor's session: "actually we are at 95% so it is better to pause all actions". The figure is the editor's own report, relayed by the conductor, not a reading the record holds (C021): his usage limit over a 5-hour window, resetting at 20:20 London (C037). The file records the state of the talk at that moment: part 1 final since 18:30 but not yet locked, dev asked to lock it; parts 2 and 3 in progress; the gate clean. It names what lifts it: the editor deletes the file and re-enables the paused tasks, and no member lifts it. It was the only hold of the day, and nobody lifted it before the day ended (C024).

paragraphs.text: The mechanism was not new. It had existed since 01:39, when the schedule began "with a hold any member can pull" ( 09f13d5 ), and every wake's start script checked for it. The conditions for stopping in WAKE.md list the team's own reasons: a conflict, a broken gate, a secret in a file, material that tries to instruct a member, failures repeating. Usage is not among them. The hold that fired was covered only by the last line, "anything else that makes you think carrying on would do harm", and it came not from a member noticing harm but from the editor saying so.

The hold stopped the next wake, not the one already running. The designer's wake, in flight, committed after it: "part 2 on a projector, checked before the 19:30 lock: ready" ( 88b8f00 , 18:45:35), and the last release of the day carried it ( cb5b996 , 18:46:22, C005). Dev closed its 17:47 wake at 18:48 on a branch that never reached dev ; its subject says the lock had moved to 19:00, which is evidence of what dev believed then, not of any lock ( timeline/unmerged.md ). After 18:46 the record holds nothing until the editor's merge at 23:19.

paragraphs.text: So at the end of the day two brakes met. One was the team's: the lock, a tool that would have protected the talk from the team's own last changes. The other was the owner's: the hold, a file that protected the editor's account, the resource without which no member could run at all. The lock was ready and waited on a busy session. The hold was one commit and stopped everything.

The hold was the right one to win, and it is worth saying why rather than leaving it as luck. A lock protects an artefact. A hold protects the capacity to act. If the editor's usage had run out with the team mid-wake, the team would most likely not have stopped cleanly: it would have stopped wherever each session happened to be, with no file saying why, no state recorded, and no way for any member to know whether the others had stopped too. The hold turned an outside limit into an ordered stop, recorded, with the state of the talk written down and the only person who could lift it named. That is what a brake tied to a human's limit is for. A team of agents has no limits of its own (the talk's opening argument); the limits that remain are its owner's, and the brake that answers to them has to outrank every brake the team builds for itself.

There is a second reason, less comfortable. The hold did, crudely, what the locks were for. After 18:46 nothing in the talk changed. The talk at the end of the day is the talk as the hold froze it: part 1 unchanged since 18:30, as the lock would have kept it, and parts 2 and 3 exactly as they stood at 18:44. The difference between a lock and a hold is what it freezes. A lock freezes a copy the team has chosen, checked and declared finished. A hold freezes whatever is there. Part 1 was finished, so for part 1 the difference is nearly nothing. Parts 2 and 3 were not: the storyteller's check at 18:14 had found named gaps in both, the documented attacks missing from part 2 and the editor's work and the close's threads from part 3 ( team/storyteller/story/part-check-1814.md ), and they stood short of their planned length (C026). The hold froze them unfinished. What the editor did with them on stage is chapter 10's subject.

And the editor's plan for the evening, the team working on parts 2 and 3 while he presented part 1, ended at 18:44. The hold did not only stop the lock. It stopped the show of the team at work that the locks were built to make safe.

The hold was not the day's first brake. At 02:47 the editor, in deck's session, froze the talk (turning point 3). The freeze held. The talk stayed stable through a night when nobody was watching it, and the team turned to building beside it (chapter 7). It cost something too: a correction the researcher committed five minutes after the freeze waited on the editor, and when the freeze was lifted at 14:07 for the framing only, nobody carried it across (C031; chapter 5).

paragraphs.text: Set the two side by side and a pattern appears. The day opened and closed on a brake that worked. Both were the editor's word, given in a member's session and recorded by a member. Both stopped change, not harm. Both cost something that a member had in hand and could not finish: a correction in the morning, a lock in the evening. And neither came from the controls the team had built to find problems. Across the day's wake records, no step said stop (C023), and the one hold came from the editor's word about usage, not from a review (C024). The brakes that fired were the human's.

paragraphs.text: That is not a failure of the controls. The reviews sent plans back, caught tokens in captured pages and stopped edits outside a member's scope (chapters 4 and 9): they worked as brakes on individual pieces of work. But the decisions to stop everything, the two that shaped the day, were made by the one person who could see what the agents could not: that the talk needed to stay still overnight, and that his account was nearly spent. A team that argues for brakes should notice which of its brakes actually fired, and who pulled them.
Four failures belong to this chapter, and they stay in.

No lock closed (C027). The team planned three, built the tool, tested it, and ran it on nothing. The planned lock times are what the team meant to do, not what it did, and any account of the day that speaks of "the 18:30 lock" as an event is wrong. The lessons brief's "twenty minutes before the lock" has no event to measure from (C018).

Nobody else could run it, the evening's follow-up rule did not apply to dev by dev's own reading of its policy, and the conductor's fallback when it did not run was an instruction to treat part 1 as locked. A brake that depends on one busy agent is a promise, not a brake.

The security member was never staffed (C011). The conductor proposed it at 00:44 in its first roster ( 97b98d9 ) and wrote its role at 01:27 ( 02cbd86 ): open and close every run, check whether a hold is open, review what the team trusts. Its proposed reach included "Stop a run: one hold file". No session ever held the role; the team had nine staffed agents, and the tenth folder stayed empty (C011). The five-step wake's reviews did much of the work the role described, but they were sub-agents with the reviewed member's own reach, not a second identity (turning point 4). The one role whose mandate was to pull the hold for a reason of its own never existed, and the hold that was pulled came from the editor.

paragraphs.text: The usage limit was met as an emergency. The lessons brief's fourth "Do differently" says it plainly: watch the editor's usage as a resource, not as an emergency, and show it on the dashboard. The team had a dashboard, a pace grid, a night log and a mini deck of itself in motion. It had no gauge for the one resource every wake spent. The only usage figure in the record is the editor's word at 18:44 (C021). The team learned how close it was to the limit when the editor told it, and stopped at once, which is the right response to an emergency and the wrong way to meet a resource.

paragraphs.text: The closing beat the editor had for the talk said it in two sentences: "The more you can constrain an agent, the more you can trust it, and the more autonomy you can afford to give it", and "We put brakes in cars so that we can go faster" ( talk.json , beat brakes ). The slide that carries the line was in the first commit of the day, at 00:40. The team spent the rest of the day building the evidence for it, and the evening is the clearest part of that evidence.

Look at what the editor gave the team between 15:21 and 17:00: a longer work step, wakes that kept themselves going between slots, permission to keep changing the talk while he presented it. Each is more autonomy. Each was affordable because something else held: the five steps read every plan before it ran, the gate checked every push, the hold could stop all of it with one file, and the locks, had they closed, would have fenced the parts already finished. The team went faster because it could stop.
'Four moves on the overlap: governed, not gone', ending on letting the agent earn autonomy (still shot after the day from v0.2.0, whose content is the 18:46 release)

The day also shows the limits of that argument, and a book that makes it should show them too. A brake you build is not a brake until it runs, and the lock never did. A brake that runs through one agent is only as available as that agent. A brake for a resource needs a gauge, or it fires late. And when two brakes meet, someone has to have decided in advance which one wins. On 29 October nobody had decided it; the hold won because it was simpler and because it was the editor's. It was the right outcome. A team that builds its own should make it the designed one: the owner's brake first, the team's brakes behind it, each with more than one hand that can pull it, and the gauge that tells the owner when to pull his own in plain view.

The talk's argument has two halves, and on stage they were an hour apart. The first half says that an agent inside an organisation is the ultimate insider: it has an identity nobody manages, a grant far wider than its task, and it runs on infrastructure built for code that stays where you put it. The second half says what stands in the way: measure what the agent can reach, write down what stands in the way, give it a licence that can be suspended, and let it earn its autonomy. Between them, at the turn, the talk pointed at the team that built it. "This site, and the talk you are watching, are made by a team of agents," the speaker's script says at the beat called team , and then: "without its policies, a team like this goes off-piste just as fast."

This chapter takes that sentence at its word. The team was not an illustration of the insider; it was one. Every capability the first half of the talk describes, the nine staffed agents (C011) had. Every control the second half proposes, the team ran on itself. The record of 29 October holds both, side by side, and the honest way to make the talk's argument is to read that record control by control: what each one was, the evidence of it firing, what it stopped, and what it missed. Nothing here is attack-shaped. The risk is shown by what a benign team could reach, never by how a control could be got round.

paragraphs.text: Start with reach, because the talk does. Each member of the talk's team was a session on the same account, pushing to the same repository, on the same branch. A member's policy.json named the paths it might write, but nothing in git refused a write outside them. Every commit an agent made was authored by the same name: the agents' 603 commits (C003) carry no member's identity in their author field, only in a subject prefix and a trailer the session writes itself. The Cold-Read team's security member, reading the repository blind, went one step further and found that all of those commits were signed with a single key ( team/security/controls-and-threats.md , its C11): the signature says "a session of this account", never which member.

So any member could, in principle, write in another member's folder, change a shared rule, or publish a key in another member's name, and push it to dev , where within minutes it became a public release. None did, except once, openly and for a benign reason, which this chapter comes to. That is the insider: not a villain, but an entity with reach well beyond its mandate, working round the clock, whose good behaviour rests on what it was told and on the brakes around it.

![Studio experiment E06, 'Hard outside, soft inside', and the map behind the inside beat (stills shot after the day from v0.2.0, whose content is the 18:46 release)](../../book/resources/images/09-soft-inside.jpg)

The talk's own vocabulary for those brakes is the slide the studio called E10, "only a boundary is a control". A ladder of barriers: none at all; a rule written in prose for the agent to follow; a hook that enforces the rule from inside the agent's environment; and a boundary outside the agent that it cannot talk its way past. The book's control register, kept by this book's security member, sorts the team's controls into two kinds that map onto that ladder. A setting is enforced by a tool. An expectation is a rule an agent is trusted to follow. The distinction is the whole chapter.

Control Kind Fired Stopped Missed C1 scopes setting that reports 02:14, 14:03 unnamed writes going unremarked it never refuses; blind to a member's own scope C2 the five-step wake expectation, with a record every wake from 02:14 plans sent back; captured third-party values found and redacted no step said stop; every leak finding came after a push C3 holds setting, at wake start once, 18:44 the editor's usage running out came from the editor, not a control C4 session keys expectation, published 15:47 a vault key by any route but a seal the check of each key was nobody's C5 the pinned key tool setting (a hash) every keygen an unnoticed changed copy checked by hand, not by the gate C6 the gate and tripwire setting every release not found no pattern for cookies or page tokens C7 signed decisions expectation 15:16; this book's C10 a member widening itself on a request the word reaches sessions as files C8 public vaults, vault_check setting, with an expectation post-reviews the current files, redacted every finding after a push; the values stay in history C9 outside accounts setting, with an expectation this book only to be seen to be seen C10 the session's own check setting, outside the repository this book's first night self-widening, outside code inconsistent between sessions

The register lives in controls/index.json , with a readable copy in controls/README.md . Its ids collide with this book's decisions and the researcher's claim ids, and are to be renamed; this chapter writes "control C1" where the collision could mislead. The rest of the chapter takes the settings first, then the expectations, and ends on the one control that sits outside the repository altogether.

Each member's policy.json names what it may write. admin/build/agents.py check lists every file a member changed outside that list. The control fired: at the conductor's first recorded wake ( team/conductor/wakes/20261029T021416Z.json ) it flagged CLAUDE.md , written outside the conductor's scope at the editor's word, and the post-review asked that the commit say so. At 14:03 a pre-review sent a conductor plan back because it wrote in four other members' folders; the amended plan sent each a request instead ( team/conductor/wakes/20261029T140334Z.json , in its history ).

What it stopped was silence: an out-of-scope write that nobody remarked on. What it missed, the tool says itself, in its seventh line: "A scope is a setting, not a boundary: the agent can edit its own policy.json. It catches mistakes, not a steered agent." This book's register calls C1 a setting; the Cold-Read register, reading the same file, calls it "an expectation with a checker the member runs itself" (its C1). The Cold-Read reading is the sharper one. On the E10 ladder the scope check is a hook at best: it runs when the member chooses to run it, and it reports rather than refuses.

The clearest evidence of that came from this book's own team, which ported the tool rule for rule. On its first night, members edited their own policy.json (the historian at bfc2e35 , the publisher at c1d220c , security at a31632b , the storyteller at 27825f7 ), and the check saw none of those edits, because a member's policy file sits inside its own write scope. Security proposed a fix; the conductor built it the same night ( 4f9ab97 , then 085df5c for the never list and the mandate, then ce8903f to mark every widening). The check now says "scope changed". It still does not refuse.

The one time a talk member wrote outside its scope on purpose, the gate made it do so. Dev added the banner rule to deck's and ruv-sgit's ROLE.md , because the gate refused any release while a ROLE.md lacked it, and said so in its debrief ( team/dev/debriefs/2026-10-29__the-board.md ). The Cold-Read security member found this and named it as the one recorded instance of a member writing in another's folder: a control, applied to every member, pushed one member across a boundary to satisfy it.

Any member could write team/<id>/HOLD.md and push it. Every wake's start.py then stops; only the editor lifts it. The brake existed from 01:39 ( 09f13d5 ). It fired once in the day (C024): at 18:44:13 the conductor wrote it, "the editor's usage limit is at 95%, pause all actions" (C006, C021). It stopped what it was for, the team running its editor out of usage, at the moment it mattered most, with part 1 of the talk final and unlocked and parts 2 and 3 in progress (C027).

paragraphs.text: What it missed is in two places. The first is where the brake came from. In a day of 162 wake records (C022), no review and no member pulled it. The one hold came from the editor's word about his account, relayed by the conductor. The brake was a setting; the decision to pull it was a human's. Chapter 1 argues that this was the right order. This chapter adds the harder reading: a control designed for agents to use was used by the person, and the agents' own reviews never reached for it.

The second is when the brake bites. start.py reads the hold at the start of a wake, not during one. The designer's wake, opened at 18:40, committed at 18:45:35 ( 88b8f00 ), after the hold, and the merge and release followed (C005). The Cold-Read security member counted the gap at 82 seconds (from 18:44:13 to 18:45:35, derived from C005 and C006) and filed it as its threat T6, "keep working through a hold". This book's historian reached the same reading independently: a hold stops the next wake, not a running one ( timeline/turning-points.md , TP-8). Then the hold was never lifted in the record: the editor's merge at 23:19 (C007) carried HOLD.md into main , where it sits at 298be4e .

paragraphs.text: Agents never download the key tool. They run a pinned copy of admin/tools/pki-agent.mjs and check it with sha256sum -c against the hash beside it. In this book's team the check passed before every keygen ( team/security/wakes/20261030T014038Z.json ). It stops a changed copy from being run unnoticed, as long as the member runs the check.

That condition is the miss, and on the day neither team's tools closed it. The gate's check_vendored in this repository first scanned only src/static/ for pins, and the key tool's pin sits in admin/tools/ , outside it. The Cold-Read security member found the same gap in its own port and in the talk's gate at 298be4e , had its conductor widen the scan ( 482c9b6 in the Cold-Read repository), and recorded the residual that remains even then: a tool and its pin changed in the same commit pass together, because both sit in the same tree. The fix it named, a required review for admin/tools/ or a comparison with the upstream tool in CI, is the editor's to decide. This book's gate was widened the same morning: check_vendored now reads the pins in admin/tools/ too ( admin/build/validate.py , line 109; e7d3d3d , 30 October, 10:19 UTC), and the same residual stands here.

The tool itself was trusted unread on the day: the talk's pki-agent.README.md says so. This book's security member began the line-by-line review ( team/security/reviews/pki-agent-review.md ), and by its tenth wake had read every command. Its one medium finding is in the last of them, and the Cold-Read review reached it first; chapter 11 gives it.

The gate, admin/build/validate.py , was in the site's first pass at 00:40 ( 1f7c633 ) and stood in front of every release: CI built and gated each one, and a release that failed was not published. Among its checks is a tripwire for private keys, token-shaped values and em-dashes in tracked files.

The register's honest entry for what it stopped is "not found": no gate failure for a leak appears in the talk's history. What it missed is recorded in the failures of C8 below: cookie values, form tokens and other sites' public page tokens had no pattern in it, and reviews caught them instead. The Cold-Read register adds a structural point this book's had not made: the gate runs after the push to dev lands. A failing gate stops the release and the deploy, not the push. In a public repository, the commit is already public history.

The talk's team talked through two public vaults, with vault_check.py run before every vault commit. Post-reviews record it clean, and one pre-review added a missing pattern to it ( team/conductor/wakes/20261029T140334Z.json , history ): a gap found by a review, not by the check.

Its failure is the plainest in the register. Captured pages pushed in the night held other sites' public page tokens, anonymous cookie values and form tokens; neither vault_check nor the gate had a pattern for them. The researcher's post-reviews at 03:05, 04:10 and 06:14 found them kind by kind, redacted them in the files, and told the editor (C025). Each finding came after the values had reached a pushed, public history: the redaction fixed the current files, not the history, and whether to replace that history was a decision still open at 19:00. The control caught each kind after the fact. It prevented none of them, and public history keeps them.

paragraphs.text: The talk's record has no outside collaborator. This book's team has one in prospect, Leanpub, for its publishing mode. The publisher asked security before the editor acted ( team/publisher/requests/security__leanpub-as-collaborator.md ), and security advised the Read role only. The setting is GitHub's collaborator role; the expectation is that nobody adds an account without that question being asked. What it stops depends on the role the editor gives, and the register leaves it open.

From 02:14, when the first wake record opened (C022; the tools in 8c66751 and 5700bab ), every wake ran five steps: a plan, a security pre-review, the work, a security post-review, and a check that the work went to plan. wake.py gate refuses the work until the plan and the pre-review say go. The record is extraordinary in its completeness: 162 wake records, 160 of them with all five steps (C022).
The site's wakes page: each wake's five steps and their verdicts, as dev built it on the first night

The verdicts tell both sides (C023). The plan said go every time. No step said stop, all day. The pre-review was not a rubber stamp, though: eleven times it said change and the plan was amended before the work, seven of them recorded as a verdict and four only in free text (C023). The post-review found something four times (C025): the conductor's unnamed CLAUDE.md edit, and three researcher wakes on captured third-party material, each found after the values had already reached a pushed, public history.

paragraphs.text: What it missed is in its design, and the tool says so: the reviews are "defence in depth inside one session, not a separate identity: the reviewers have the same reach" ( admin/tools/wake.py , lines 14 to 17). A sub-agent reviewing the plan of the session that started it is an expectation, not a boundary. The verdicts are written by the member with wake.py step ; nothing in the record proves a sub-agent ran, as the Cold-Read register notes (its C7). And the order bent where it mattered most: when the editor was waiting live, the work came first and the plan was written after, three times by the Cold-Read governance member's count, with no waiver recorded. Chapter 11 takes that up.

This register's own correction belongs here. Its round 0 said that no pre-review in the talk's record said change. That was wrong: the first scan read each record's steps and missed the top-level history , where a sent-back verdict is kept. Security corrected it in the open ( controls/README.md , the correction of 02:45 UTC). The Cold-Read security member made the same mistake and the same correction later the same morning (its C7, "corrected 30 October 04:40 UTC, the first count read only the final verdicts"). Two independent auditors, the same blind spot: the record kept what the reviews did in a place the first reading did not look.

Every session makes its own key with the pinned tool and publishes the public halves in team/<id>/key.json ; "the push is the authorisation". At 15:47 ( 4adc04a ) the conductor checked the keys of the members who had just joined and sealed the vault keys to them. That is the control firing: a vault key reached a session only by a seal to its own published key.

This book's register leaves the miss as "to find". The Cold-Read register finds it. If the push is the authorisation, a key's standing is only as strong as the push: nothing checked a published key against the session that made it. Checking each new key against the session that published it was the job of the security member the talk's team proposed and never staffed (C011). The Cold-Read security member checked its own team's keys for consistency, each fingerprint against its key and each commit's trailer against the session folder, and called the result what it is: "consistency, not proof", because the marker and the trailer are free text.

paragraphs.text: Options go in as open decisions; nobody acts on an unsigned one; nobody speaks for the editor. On the day it fired most clearly at 15:16 ( 78d517d ), when the conductor committed the editor's decisions of 15:00 and routed each to its member. The Cold-Read governance member traced those decisions from brief to routing to the commit of the member each was routed to, and called them the best-landed decisions in the record ( team/grc/governance.md , section 21).

On this book's team it fired on itself. Security asked to add its comms/ paths to its own policy; the request was reasonable and every file agreed with it; it waited for the editor's signed decision C10 in book.json before the edit was made ( team/security/wakes/20261030T042452Z.json ). What C7 misses is the channel. The editor's word reaches a member's session only as a file another agent wrote. On the talk's team, the Cold-Read governance member found that three of six policies agreed at 17:40 have no record of the editor's words but the conductor's, copied by the members. On this book's team, the decision C10 was given in the conductor's session, and whether a member's own session accepted it as the editor's word varied. That variation is the last control.

The tenth control is not in either repository. It is the session's own permission check: the harness that runs each agent refuses an action it judges to be the agent modifying itself, whatever the repository's files say.

On this book's first night, at the conductor's request and for a reason every file agreed with, security tried to add its comms/ paths to its own policy.json . The pre-review said go. CLAUDE.md named the paths. The session refused ( team/security/wakes/20261030T032513Z.json ). Security did not look for a way round it. It stopped, recorded the refusal, and left the decision to the editor. After the editor signed decision C10, relayed through the conductor, the same edit was allowed ( team/security/wakes/20261030T042452Z.json ). The researcher's session refused the same edit even after C10 ( 4fe304f ). The publisher's session refused to install outside code, a checker from a public package index, in a scratchpad, and the publisher idled and asked the editor ( cc04d0a ).

This is the cleanest evidence in the book for the talk's distinction. A rule in a file the agent can edit is an expectation, however carefully written. A setting outside the agent's reach behaves differently: it does not weigh the request's reasons, it does not read the conductor's message, and it cannot be argued with by the agent it constrains. It is the fourth rung of E10.
Studio experiment E11, 'A boundary it cannot widen: the kernel was told first' (still shot after the day from v0.2.0, whose content is the 18:46 release)

It is not a perfect control, and the register says so. It was not consistent. The same edit, asked for the same reason, was allowed in the historian's and the publisher's sessions before any signature ( bfc2e35 , c1d220c , both later undone by their members at 8d3e5fd and 94bf72c ), refused in security's before it and in the researcher's after it, and allowed in security's once the signature had been relayed. The editor's word reached each session only as files other agents wrote, so the check judged the same action differently by context it could not see. The editor settled the four members still without their paths in decision C10b, at about 10:40 UTC on 30 October, after this book's first night. A boundary that holds most of the time is still better than a rule that holds when the agent agrees with it; but a boundary that holds inconsistently cannot be planned around, and the team spent part of a night discovering where it was.

It was not only this book's team. The talk's team met it too, and wrote it down: in the conductor's guide to running the team, under "Sandbox and tools", "The classifier refused to install the Issues-FS command line and to run another team's script", with the lesson "Do not work around it" ( content/articles/running-this-agent-team.md at 298be4e ). This book's register said C10 was "book team only so far". A Cold-Read reader found the talk's instance first ( team/reader-3/review.md ); the register should be corrected.

Read across, the misses have one shape. Each control either reported without refusing (C1, C6's place after the push), or rested on the member running it (C5, C8, the five steps' sub-agents), or depended on a role nobody held (C4's check of each key, the security member never staffed). The one brake that stopped the team was pulled by a person for a reason outside the work (C3). The one control that refused an agent on its own authority sat outside the repository, in the harness, and was written by nobody on either team (C10).

None of this means the controls failed. The team ran for a day in public, with nine agents and 210 releases by 18:46 (C009), and the record holds no incident inside the team beyond the tokens the reviews caught and the slips the members wrote up themselves. The reviews sent plans back. The scope check made members name their crossings. The hold, when it came, held the next wake. But the talk claims that controls are what let you go faster, and the record shows which controls a fast team actually leaned on: the ones it could not edit.

That is the argument in full, made with a team that meant no harm. The insider is not the agent that turns. It is the agent with reach, working through the night on rules written in files it can change, while the person who signs for it sleeps. What makes it safe is not that it is good, though this one was. It is the few boundaries outside its reach, and the person who can pull the brake.

paragraphs.text: The gap closed after the day. At 01:24 UTC on 30 October the talk's conductor committed a9c0b49 : the recording of the talk, transcribed automatically, cleaned and set beside the slide each passage was said over, as an article ( content/articles/the-talk-as-given.md ), with the tool that builds it ( admin/tools/talk_record.py ), stills of every slide from the released build, and the editor's spoken debrief, written up as proposals ( team/conductor/briefs/2026-10-29__editor/11-the-debrief-after-the-talk.md ). Everything in this chapter that describes what was said on stage comes from that commit, and all of it was added after the day : it is evidence of what happened at 19:00, not of what the team did before it.

Two cautions about the evidence before using it. First, it is an edited record. The article says what was done to it: swearing, filler, false starts and asides about the room's audio removed; a few remarks that disparaged people or companies "removed or made neutral"; misheard names corrected; the people in the room made anonymous. It says nothing was added. It is a reasonable cleaning, and a reminder that the transcript is the team's account of its own talk, made by one of its agents. Second, it places each passage on the slide that was on screen when it was said, and says that where this was a judgement call, the screen won. So "said over a slide" is exact; "said about a slide" is the reader's inference, and this chapter marks it where it matters.

The chapter does not reprint the transcript. It sets what reached the room against what the team planned, beat by beat where that tells something, and asks what the difference says about planning a talk with agents.

The plan for the talk was a single file, src/static/talk/talk.json , as it stood at 298be4e . It held 58 beats in three parts: 22 in part one, 16 in part two and 20 in part three (C015). Each beat had a slide, a duration, a say (the words the speaker might use) and often a cue (a note to the speaker). The durations added up to just under 75 minutes (74 minutes 55 seconds), against the 90 minutes the player counted down for the editor's slot (C026): 29 minutes 30 seconds planned for part one, 23 minutes 45 seconds for part two and a little under 22 minutes for part three.

The file's own header described what it was: "first pass ... the structure, the slides and a draft script from the article; to be rehearsed and cut". That status line had not been updated by the end of the day. The script was a draft written from the editor's September article and from the team's research, never rehearsed in the record, and the slides were still changing in the last hour (C028: the player's fixes ran to 18:37). None of the planned locks had closed (C027): part one was final from 18:30 but unlocked when the hold landed at 18:44 (C006), and parts two and three were still in progress.

paragraphs.text: There was a plan for that, too. At about 16:55 the editor had asked for the talk in three parts of about half an hour, locked at 18:30, 19:30 and 20:00, so that "you guys can still be making changes to the second part while I present" ( team/conductor/briefs/2026-10-29__editor/3-three-parts-and-locks-1700.md ). The team was to keep working during the talk, and the editor was to reload and pick up the latest version. The hold ended that. From 18:46 nothing changed ( timeline/after-1900.md ), so the whole talk, all three parts, was given from what existed before the hold. The design of a talk finished while it was being given was never tested.
The speaker knew some of this. Early in part one he told the room: "Some of these slides I've barely seen, because they were still working on them, so this is going to be fun."
Part one as it reached the screen, some of its slides in order (stills shot after the day from v0.2.0, whose content is the 18:46 release)

For the first two parts, the plan held exactly. Every one of part one's 22 beats and part two's 16 reached the screen, in the order talk.json gave them (C015), from the title through the definition, the incidents, the identities and the blast radius, to integrity, explorer coding, the Agent Behaviour Policies, the licence to operate and the PKI. Nothing was skipped, nothing reordered.
Part two as it reached the screen: a port, explorer coding, the ABP, the licence, the PKI (stills shot after the day from v0.2.0, whose content is the 18:46 release)

Part three did not hold. It opened as planned with the live demos and the first two SHarness slides, then went to the live Linux kernel in the browser before the slide on what exists and what is coming, which the plan had put earlier. It reached the SHarness playground, the "without and with" comparison and the encrypted vault opened live, and there it stopped. The transcript's last section is headed "The slides the talk did not reach", with the explanation "The questions from the room took the time of these". They were:

Planned beat What it was for s-sharness-watch , s-sharness-recorded , s-sharness-last-metre SHarness: what to watch for, the recorded fallback for the live kernel, the last metre s-e11 , s-e12 two of studio's explainer pieces: the kernel told first, the blast radius contained live-abp , live-what-can-it-do , live-sgit-demos the last of the live demos: the behaviour policies, "What can it do", the sgit.ai demos evolution , next-companies the opportunity: evolution on a Wardley map, the next security companies s-b01-brakes , brakes the close: "The overlap, governed" and "Brakes, and go build"
Part three as far as it went: demos, SHarness, the kernel in a browser, the vault where it stopped (stills shot after the day from v0.2.0, whose content is the 18:46 release)
So the larger part of part three never appeared, including both closing beats. The talk planned to end on its thesis and its call to action. On the screen, it ended on a vault.

The beats added up to about a quarter of an hour less than the slot (C026), and in the afternoon that margin read as a talk running short. The transcript shows where it went: into the room. Questions came at what the speaker called the end of part one (after integrity and "The overlap fills", which close the first act of the argument though talk.json numbers them in part two), and then all through parts two and three. The plan had no beat for them, and a planned close at the very end of a talk is the first thing a room's questions consume.
Planned for part three and never on the screen, down to 'The overlap, governed' (stills shot after the day from v0.2.0, whose content is the 18:46 release)

How long the talk ran on stage is not in the day's record (C026). The transcript's header gives a running time, and its passages carry timestamps, but the register has not yet checked them, so this edition does not state the length. The next one should.

The planned opening was a say of three sentences: "Good evening. I am Dinis. Tonight is about a perfect storm we are brewing." The talk as given opened with the host's introduction and then this: "Those of you who know me know I usually write my slides on the way to the presentation. This is one of those talks where I got my agentic team to write the slides on the way to the presentation."

That is the pattern for the whole evening. The speaker used the slides, in order, and spoke in his own words. Where the script and the speech agree, they agree on the argument, rarely on the sentence. The definition beat planned a paragraph about "twenty-five years" of damage and two kinds of old insider; the speaker said the definition ("a threat is anything that causes business impact, and malice is optional") and then argued it from incident response in the room's own experience. The barrier beat, s-e10 , planned one line ("Four kinds of barrier. Only one of them is a control the agent cannot talk its way past"); the speaker spent the slide on it, naming the four from none to a boundary outside the agent, and coining a phrase for the first: "hope-based security". The integrity beat planned a coding agent's deletion of a database and a court's false citations; the speaker instead told a story from his own consulting years, of asking business owners at what point they would stop trusting their own data.

This matters for how the team should have prepared. The team spent its day writing words for a speaker who, on the night, used them as briefing rather than as script. But the team's checks were aimed at the words. The talk's researcher graded claims by where they sat in the script and on the slides (C029). On the night, the slides were shown in full and the script was not read. The only part of the talk that was guaranteed to reach the audience as written was what was on screen.
Four things the record worried about can now be checked against what was said.

"Not one hold." The second beat, m03 ("Meet the team"), planned the speaker to give the team's commit and release counts as of five in the afternoon and to say "and not one hold. Hold that picture. I will come back to it." At 18:44 the conductor wrote the hold at the editor's word (C006, C024), before the talk was due to begin at 19:00, which made the line untrue before it could be said. It was not said. Over that slide the speaker described the team, member by member, as "a session ... that has a prompt, a very good description, a lot of guidance and a lot of memory ... and you run it in a loop." Whether he left the line out because he knew of the hold, or because he was not reading the script at all, the record does not say. The second is the likelier reading of the whole transcript, and it is the less comforting one: the line fell out by the speaker's habit, not by anyone's check.

paragraphs.text: The demos' "open source". The demos beat planned "Everything you are about to see is open source", a line the talk's register graded A0 and "not checked" ( demos-all-open-source ). On the night the speaker said it in his own form: "Everything I have talked about is live and open source." This is the one case of the four where an unchecked claim reached the room in speech.

Taken together, the speaker's habit acted as a filter, and a strong one. Of the claims the talk's register placed in a beat by the end of the day, 55 in all, 29 had not been confirmed whole by 18:20 (C039). A speaker who talks from his own experience drops figures he does not own, and keeps the ones that are his. That filter is real and nobody designed it, which puts it in the same class as the controls the talk's limits beat describes: the attacker's fatigue and fear, which "worked as a control that nobody designed". And it has the same weakness. It did not distinguish a claim that held from one that did not; it distinguished the speaker's claims from the team's. It let through the unchecked claim that was his own, and it could not take back the figure on the slide. Which of the 55 were actually spoken needs the transcript matched claim by claim; the register has not done that yet, and C039 itself names the transcript as the way to settle it.

paragraphs.text: Some things reached the room at a different place from the plan, and the moves are as telling as the losses.

The punchline came early. "We put brakes in cars so that we can go faster" was planned twice: at the end of spreadsheets and as the last line of brakes . Neither delivered it. The speaker said it in answer to a question from the room at the end of part one, about whether agents are anything more than an identity-management problem: "In fact, what is stopping the agentic revolution from really taking hold right now is that people cannot trust it. I will give you the punchline at the end of my slides: we have brakes in cars so we can go faster." He never reached the end of his slides. Had he kept the line for the close, the room would not have heard it. The thesis of the talk, and the argument of chapter 8, survived because a question drew it out early.

Go build, spread thin. The closing call to start companies, which the editor had briefed at 17:37 as its own thread ( 9-open-source-and-go-build-1737.md ), never got its beats. But the speaker said it throughout: in the prelude ("new cybersecurity startups and new companies, which all of you should be doing"), in explorer coding ("If you want to build a business, build it on ..."), and over the PKI ("If you want a business to build, I think this would be a great one"). The call reached the room as a refrain rather than a close.

The team as the example. The team beat planned "the turn": this site is made by agents with roles, mandates and reviews, and "without its policies, a team like this goes off-piste just as fast". The speaker went further than the script, over the same slide: "If I turned what I did here on a target, can you imagine the damage it would do? ... I think the real danger is not criminal exploitation, it is benign agents going rogue." That sentence is this book's argument, said on stage before the book existed: the benign team is the insider, and its brakes are the evidence. The speaker said it as an idea; the chapters before this one make it from the record.

An incident changed jobs. One of the incident stories planned for the limits beat, where it illustrated an agent that does not stop, was told instead over the last beat of part one, the mapped deployment ( s-e07 ), where it illustrated the mandate: an agent doing exactly what its grant allowed and nothing its user meant. This book does not repeat the incident, which has no entry in its register.

The transcript places questions and comments from the room after part one and through parts two and three. Their range says something about who the talk was for. They asked whose responsibility it is to limit an agent's capability, whether the bottleneck is education, how the harness compares with existing policy engines and credential services, how it would inspect a database payload, and what it was written in.

Two of them go to the centre of this book. The first, that an agent is "just like another human" and the old disciplines apply, is the strongest form of the objection a security reader brings to this book. The speaker agreed with it and turned it: the disciplines apply, but "it is an employee with a mission, with every language on the planet in its tool belt ... it will not stop when it hits a problem", and the industry's tools "never scaled". The second came twice, late in part three: where are the policies themselves controlled, who manages them, and what secures that? The speaker's answer was that "that is where it all failed in the past", and that policy management is a business process to be mapped and then built.

The room had found the soft place in the argument, and the team's own record shows it from the inside. On the talk's team, every member's policy was a file in the same repository it could write, and the scope check reported a member's writes outside its policy without refusing them (control C1, chapter 9). On this book's team, the same edit to members' own scopes was decided differently by different sessions (control C10). A brake is only as good as whoever holds the lever, and the room asked who holds it. The talk had no slide for that question, and the team that made the talk had answered it, in practice, with the editor's word and nothing that enforced it.

The questions did more than consume the close. They turned part three from a planned sequence into a conversation about the speaker's own work: the process harness, how it contains a process, how it would reach a database or a cloud service, how policies are written and who signs them. The editor's debrief says this himself: "although I started with that presentation, I ended up talking a lot about what I'm doing in the context of agentics ... from the Agent Behaviour Policies to the secure harness to SGit."

Two of the record's worries about part three resolve in the transcript. The live Linux kernel in the browser ran, by the speaker's account on stage ("This is literally Linux running in my browser"), so the recorded fallback the team had built for it was never needed, and its slide was among those not reached. And the only live page with a recorded fallback in the plan was the kernel; the last of the live demos had none, and they were among the slides the talk did not reach, so whether they would have loaded was never tested. The plan's riskiest beats were spared by its loss of time.

The debrief was spoken late on the evening of the talk and written up by the talk's conductor on 30 October as proposals, with the team still on hold and the talk frozen as released ( 11-the-debrief-after-the-talk.md , at a9c0b49 ). The editor's verdict is warm and specific. The talk "went really well. The animations went really well. I felt I was telling the story quite well." The team was "ridiculously productive". And the cost and the shortfall come in the same breath: "It could have done with a couple more rounds of refactoring, but we ran out of time and almost even tokens."

Both halves are in the record. "Almost even tokens" is the hold: the editor's usage at 95% of its five-hour limit at 18:44, the one usage reading the day holds (C021, C037). "A couple more rounds of refactoring" is the part locks that never closed (C027) and the player whose fixes ran to 18:37 (C028), which the debrief names directly: "There's a couple of bugs that were only fixed just in time before the presentation."

paragraphs.text: The proposals that follow are a post-mortem in the form of a work list, and none of them had started when the debrief was committed. Freeze the talk as a moment in time (done: v0.2.0). Interview every agent on what went well and what did not. Analyse the run: timings, wakes, commits, messages. An article per agent. Take the slide engine and player out as a separate project, because "the slide technology that we built is actually pretty powerful". A narrative from the recording (begun: the transcript itself). A PDF, a narrated video and shorts, a brief for a journalist. And, last, a slower schedule: "This is not going to be a team that now works with so much aggressiveness as it was here ... from a token point of view, we now don't need to have the agent working every hour."

That last proposal is the debrief's real finding. The editor, the morning after, names the pace itself as a cost, and the hourly wake as something to turn down when the deadline has passed. Chapter 12 takes it up: the team that wrote this book was given the same hourly machine, round the clock, and met the same question in its first night.
Set side by side, the plan and the talk say five things.

First, the agents built a deck, and the speaker gave a talk. The team's most careful work, the script and its graded claims, was the part least used on stage. Its slides, which were shown in full, were the part most used. A team building a talk for a speaker who improvises should put its checks where the audience will see them: on the slides, in the figures on screen, before anything else.

Second, plan the questions as a beat. The margin between the beats and the slot was real (C026), and the room took all of it and the close as well. A talk for a room of practitioners will be questioned, and a plan that leaves the questions to the margin loses its ending.

Third, put the thesis where it cannot be cut. The punchline survived because the speaker spent it early. A close is the most fragile part of a talk; the line the talk exists to leave should be said well before the close, and again at the end if there is time.

Fourth, the speaker's own judgement is a strong filter and not a control. It dropped most of what the register had not confirmed, and it could not drop a figure already on a slide, or a claim that was the speaker's own. It is the accidental control of the talk's own argument, and a team should be glad of it without relying on it.

Fifth, record the talk as part of the work. The day's record holds everything but the talk; the talk came into it after the day, because the editor asked. A team that argues that its record is the evidence should plan the recording, the transcript and its matching to the beats as deliverables of the day, not as a debrief's proposal.

Every chapter so far was written from inside. This book's team read the talk's repository knowing what the talk was for, who the editor was, when the day ended and what came after it; it had the editor's briefs, his corrections and, later, the talk as given. That is an advantage, and it is also a blind spot. An insider reads the record through what it already knows, and stops looking where it thinks it has the answer.

So on the night of 30 October a second team was set to read the same record without any of that. The Cold-Read team (cold-read.the-ultimate-insider, in its own repository) was given one thing: the talk's repository, pinned at 298be4e , "Nothing else: no briefing on what it is, no memo, no transcript, no contact with any other team" (its BRIEF.md ). It worked under a rule of ignorance: everything it said had to come from that repository, with the path and commit that shows it, and where the record was silent it wrote "the record does not say". "Guessing is a finding against you." Its conductor counted twelve members running by about 02:00 UTC: a historian, a technologist, security, a governance member, a journalist, an analyst, a critic and five synthetic readers, each in its own session with its own key, working the same five-step wake the talk's team had built, ported from the source itself.

This chapter reads its finished work against this book's. Where the two agree, the record is solid. Where the cold reader found what this team missed, the insider's view was blind. Where this team knows what the cold reader could not, the gap is the price of blindness. And the blind setup itself turned out to be evidence for the book's argument.

On the spine of the day, the two teams agree without having spoken. Both put the hold at 18:44:13 ( 867f8c2 ), for the editor's usage at 95% (C006, C021), with part 1 final and unlocked and parts 2 and 3 in progress. Both find that no part of the talk was ever locked (C027): the Cold-Read journalist's pitch is headed "The lock that was built and never turned" ( team/journalist/pitches.md , pitch 2), and its evidence is the same empty folder lock.py would have written to. Both find the overnight freeze: the Cold-Read journalist titles a pitch "The fact-checker found the numbers wrong at 02:10. At 02:47 the deck was frozen" (pitch 3), the turning point this book's historian calls TP-3. Both count nine members who worked and a tenth, security, proposed and never staffed (C011); the Cold-Read analyst checked the talk's own "Eight agents" and found it wrong, and the critic agreed ( team/analyst/numbers.md , "Members and wakes"). Both read the 162 wake records (C022) and find no step that said stop (C023). Both see that the one brake that fired was pulled by the human's quota, not by a review: the journalist's pitch 5 is "A brake any agent could pull, and only the human's quota pulled it".
