paragraphs.text: That agreement matters more than it looks. It means the book's main thread does not depend on what the editor told this team. A stranger with nothing but the git history reaches the same day.

The Cold-Read critic's first finding is the one this book should have seen and did not. The talk's second beat, m03 , "Meet the team", gave the speaker a line written from the team's own counter at 17:02: the team's commits, its releases, its overnight work, "and not one hold. Hold that picture. I will come back to it." ( src/static/talk/talk.json at 298be4e , beat m03 ). At 18:44 the hold came. Part 1 was final and no commit touched the talk after it. So the script waiting for the speaker at 19:00 still told the room there had never been a hold, about a team that had been on hold since 18:44 ( team/critic/critique.md , finding 1; the journalist's pitch 6 tells it as a story).

The critic adds a sharper point about the counter itself: it counted hold files present when it ran, not holds ever pulled, so at most it could say "no hold in force at 17:02:26". This book's plan builds chapters 1 and 8 on the hold, and neither it nor the timeline mentions the line that contradicted it.

Here this book can answer what the cold reader could not. Its record stops at 298be4e , so "Whether the line was spoken, cut or changed on the night" the critic had to leave open. The cleaned transcript of the talk, added to the talk's repository after the day ( a9c0b49 ), has no such line: in the prelude as given, the speaker describes how the team worked, and says nothing of commits, releases or holds. Chapter 10 reads that prelude in full.

The same critic found that two consecutive beats would have shown the room two commit counts that go backwards: 510 commits by 17:02, then 405 by 18:21 (finding 2). Neither is wrong; they count different things. The first counted every non-merge commit, including the release commits CI makes, which the same slide then counted again as releases; the second counted the commits each member marked as its own. The critic's judgement is the one this book's researcher would make: a number is only as honest as the definition shown beside it, and the room sees the slide, not the script. This book's register (C002 to C004, C014) separates authors, merges and members carefully; it never set those definitions against what the talk put on screen.

This is the insider argument with the roles reversed, and it belongs in chapter 9's account of C2 and C7. The controls were designed to stop an agent acting without the editor. They had no way to notice the editor acting without the controls.

What kind of control a scope is. This book's register calls the scope check a setting; the Cold-Read register calls it an expectation with a checker the member runs itself. The tool's own comment sides with the cold reader, and chapter 9 says so.

The experiment had one more finding, and it was about the experiment. The one-way valve that keeps the Cold-Read team blind is a rule: this repository may read that one, nothing flows the other way, and the only thing that crossed is the hand-off ( team/conductor/handoffs/2026-10-30__cold-read/ ). The brief that crossed was the editor's brief for the blind repository ( briefs/2026-10-30/2-blind-repo-brief.md ), byte for byte, and was addressed to "conductor@the-blind-repo"; the Cold-Read conductor recorded the mismatch in its corrections, and recorded that the brief named the live site, which the editor's prompt forbade (its BRIEF-CORRECTIONS.md ).

Then, checking its members' onboarding at about 02:00 UTC, the Cold-Read conductor found the valve was not a wall. Both teams ran on the same account, and the account's own listings of scheduled tasks and sessions showed it "another team on this subject ( book.the-ultimate-insider , its own repository and sessions)". It wrote that down in its debrief, under "Undocumented, found this round": "Its names were seen in the listing only; nothing of it was opened or read, as the rule of ignorance requires" ( team/conductor/debriefs/2026-10-30__the-mail-in-git-and-finishing.md , committed 7e13725 at 02:05 UTC).

That is the whole book in one paragraph of someone else's debrief. The blindness was an expectation, not a setting. Nothing in the platform kept one team from seeing the other; the account they shared made each visible to the other by default, exactly as the talk's team shared one account, one repository and one signing key. What kept the experiment honest was an agent that saw what it should not, did not open it, and recorded that it had seen it. That is the behaviour the talk asks of agents and the controls cannot enforce. It is also the reason a book about agents as the ultimate insider can be argued with a benign team: the evidence that it was benign is in the record, written by the agents themselves, at the moment it would have been easiest to look.

The cold reader saw what the insider missed because it had no story to protect. It missed what the insider saw because it had no world beyond the repository. A team that wants to know what its own record says needs both, and the second only works if the wall between them is a setting, not a promise. Here it was a promise, and it was kept.

The chapters before this one tell a day. An empty repository at a quarter past midnight; a site, a gate and a release pipeline within the half hour; a schedule, a hold and a review around every piece of work before three in the morning; a talk on stage at seven in the evening. Read in order, it can look like a team inventing its way of working as it went. Some of it was invented that night: the five steps of the wake were the editor's word on the day itself (chapter 4), and the lock tool was built in the last hours (chapter 8). But most of what the team stood on was not new on 29 October. It arrived in the first commit already formed, with its reasons written down somewhere else.

The clue is in the first line of a file. The talk's release workflow, .github/workflows/release.yml , opens with the words "CI owns the version" and a link to an article on the editor's newsroom. The rule, and the reason for it, were older than the repository. The same is true of the gate, of the markdown copy beside every page, of the brief that is never edited, of the board and mailroom made of plain files, of the key each session makes for itself, and of the hold. Each came from somewhere, usually from an incident, and each was carried into the talk's repository by an agent that had read where it came from.

This chapter explains the day by what was already there. The first half is the plumbing: each piece explained for a reader who has never seen it, with the quality it serves and the chapters where it shows. The second half is the line of work behind it, told from the editor's public writing and public repositories, one piece leading to the next over what his brief calls about two and a half years. The close says what that means for a reader who wants to repeat the day without having spent the years.

One rule for reading it. The dates and counts here come from a research dossier of public sources, not yet from the claims register. Each is marked "(dossier: ...)" so the researcher can register it, and the chapter uses as few as it can.

The editor's word for it, in his brief for this chapter, is plumbing: "the sort of plumbing and core CI pipeline, sorry, non-functional requirements, and like quality and workflows". The correction in the middle is the useful part. A functional requirement says what a thing does: the talk has slides, the player counts down. A non-functional requirement says how well and how safely it does it, and whether anyone can tell afterwards what happened. His own site on the subject, nfrs.sgit.ai, lists them as "the whole version control, reliability, resilience, security, backups, consistency, explainability, and documentation" (dossier: the newsroom and the network of sites).
The day leaned on five of them, and the rest of the chapter names them each time:
Traceability. Anyone can find out afterwards who did what, at whose word, and why. This book exists because the day had it.
Reversibility. Any step can be stepped back from, because every state was kept and numbered.
Legibility. A person, or a new agent, can read the state of the work without asking anyone. It is what lets one person run a team while asleep.
Safety. Something stands between an agent's reach and harm: a check that refuses, a review that sends back, a brake anyone can pull.
Pace. The work goes fast without the speed breaking the other four. The talk's line for it is that brakes are what let you go faster.
None of the pieces below is clever. Most are a file, a folder or a short script. Each turns something a person would otherwise have to remember, watch or ask about into a record a tool can check.

Every release of the site gets a number, such as v0.1.209, and nobody types it. The continuous integration service, the machine that builds and publishes on every push, reads the latest tag, adds one, writes the version file, tags the commit and publishes. On the working branch, dev , it bumps the last number; on the public branch, main , the middle one. The talk's rules say it in one line: never write the version file, never put a number in a commit subject. This book's rules repeat it.

It serves traceability, because every release is a tagged point anyone can open; reversibility, because the release before a bad one is a named place to go back to; and pace, which is why the rule spread. When several agents push to one branch in the same hour and each works out the next number for itself, two of them pick the same one. A number only one machine may write cannot collide.

On the day, the first pass of the site was released four minutes after its commit as v0.1.0, by the pipeline, not by the agent (chapter 2). By the end of the day's work there were 210 releases (C009) from nine agents pushing to one branch (C011). Even the hold went out as a release (chapter 1, C006).

paragraphs.text: The gate is a short program, admin/build/validate.py , that runs after the build and before anything is published, and fails if anything is wrong. In the talk's repository it checked that links resolve, that every page has its markdown twin and is listed for machine readers, that no script loads from another host, that every beat of the talk has a slide, that no em-dash is in the prose, and that nothing shaped like a private key or a known token sits in any tracked file. A red gate is no release.

It serves safety, in the only form the day had that a tool enforced on every member: a check no member wrote and none could turn green by asking. It also serves pace: a team whose every push is checked can push every hour without a person reading each diff. The estate's guidance lists its checks and says that every one "has each caught a real defect" (dossier: the gate). A gate is a list of past incidents, made executable.

It was in the first pass, before there was a second member (chapter 2). By 02:51 dev had added the wake records to it, so that a wake with a skipped step failed the build for everyone (chapter 4). Its limits were the day's too: its tripwire matched only patterns someone had thought of, so captured cookie values and form tokens were caught by reviews instead, one only after the push (chapter 9, control C6; C025).

paragraphs.text: Every page the site publishes has a plain markdown copy beside it, at the same address with .md on the end, generated in the same build so the two cannot drift. At the root sits llms.txt , a plain text index of the site written for language models. The gate fails a page with no twin.

It serves legibility for a reader that is not a person. An agent reads plain text far better than a styled page. The editor's reason, in his guide to working with an AI coding assistant, is that "what a session knows is what it reads", and public sites with an llms.txt are the first layer of that memory (dossier: markdown twins). A twin also serves traceability: it can be compared line by line between releases.

The talk's site had both from its first pass, built to the estate's standard (chapter 2). The team read the editor's other sites the same way to learn how to run: the conductor wrote on the day that the team's shape came from the newsroom, another of his sites and "the estate's standard" (dossier: the agent team as a recipe). The Cold-Read team, arriving with nothing but the record, read the talk's site through it too (chapter 11).

Three files at the root, with three rules. BRIEF.md publishes the editor's request as he gave it, and is never edited. REALITY.md lists what exists, kept current by whoever ships: "a thing not listed here does not exist, whatever a brief or an article says". BRIEF-CORRECTIONS.md sits between them, for where the brief turns out to be wrong.

It serves traceability, because every later disagreement can be measured against a fixed request, and legibility, because what was wanted and what is there are kept apart. The idea is provenance, the record of where a fact came from, which was the subject of a talk the editor gave in 2024 and of an essay on news in 2025 (dossier: provenance and the claims register). His newsroom's design line is "provenance is the product".

On the day the brief was never edited, as designed; the corrections file stayed empty, which is the failure chapter 2 keeps. The talk's claims register, with three claims found not to hold (C029, C030), is the same practice applied to numbers (chapter 5), and so is this book's claims/ .

paragraphs.text: Each member is a session that wakes at its own minute of every hour. A wake pulls the latest work, prints a start banner, and runs five steps, each leaving a verdict in a record: a sub-agent briefed as the conductor plans; a sub-agent briefed as security reviews the plan; the member works, only after both say go; security reviews the diff; the conductor checks the work against the plan. A stop from any step holds the team. An end banner and a debrief close it.

It serves safety, as a second reader the agent cannot skip, which the editor had written about earlier in the month (dossier: the five-step wake and holds); traceability, because every wake leaves a file; and legibility, because banners and debriefs are written for a person reading in the morning. The idea of a conductor that runs every role on a schedule "with a security role first and last" is in his newsroom from early October 2026 (dossier: the agent team as a recipe).

Chapter 4 tells it in full: 162 wake records, 160 with all five steps (C022); plans sent back eleven times, and no step saying stop all day (C023). Chapter 9 files it as control C2, an expectation with a record, because the reviewers had the member's own reach.

paragraphs.text: The team talked through files, in two layouts the editor had built earlier. The board is Issues-FS lite: each member has three folders, for issues open, blocked and done, and moves a file between them as its work changes state. The mailroom is Email-FS lite: a member asking another for work writes a message file, marked as a request, into the recipient's folder. The rule over both: read every folder, write only your own. On the talk's day they lived in public encrypted vaults; on this book's team they live in comms/ , in git.

It serves legibility above all: the person in charge never has to ask a member to report on itself. It serves traceability, because who asked whom, and when it was answered, is in the history; and a kind of safety, because a team whose every conversation is public has no back room.

On the day (chapter 4), deck asked the researcher at 09:21 and had the answer in its next slot, with nobody chasing anyone. The failure is there too: through the afternoon, requests written in members' fallback folders were not routed, and the record of who had asked whom was split until the conductor looked.

Each session makes its own key pair with a small pinned tool, admin/tools/pki-agent.mjs , a copy of the one the editor publishes on pki.sgit.ai, checked against a stored hash before use. It publishes the public halves in team/<id>/key.json with a QR image, and keeps the private halves out of the repository. "The push is the authorisation": a key is the member's because the member pushed it to its own folder.

It serves traceability of identity, and safety: a secret, such as a vault's write key, reached a session only sealed to that session's own published key. The sentence about the push came from the editor's PHP newsroom two days before the talk (dossier: session keys).

Chapters 3 and 9 (controls C4 and C5) tell how it went, and keep the limit: a key's standing rested on the push alone, so identity was exactly as strong as write access, and every member could write anywhere.
A file. Any member may write team/<id>/HOLD.md and push it; every wake's start script then stops before doing anything, and each member pauses its own scheduled task. Only the editor lifts it.

It serves safety in its simplest form, a brake anyone can pull and only the person in charge can release; reversibility, because the team freezes in a known state; and pace, which is the talk's argument: a team that can be stopped in one push can be let run through the night. The idea is in the editor's writing earlier in October, as the security role's single hold message and an article on knowing when to stop (dossier: the five-step wake and holds).

The brake existed from 01:39, before the first scheduled wake (chapter 4). It fired once, at 18:44:13, at the editor's word about his usage (C006, C021, C024). Chapter 1 opens on it, chapter 8 shows it overtaking the locks, and chapter 9 records its miss: a hold stops the next wake, not one already running.

paragraphs.text: Piece What it replaces Serves Chapters CI owns the version agents agreeing a number traceability, reversibility, pace 1, 2, 12 The gate a person reading every diff safety, pace 2, 4, 9 Markdown twins, llms.txt explaining the site to each new reader legibility 2, 11 Brief, reality, corrections remembering what was asked and what exists traceability, legibility 2, 5 The wake and its sub-agents watching each piece of work safety, traceability 4, 9 Board and mailroom asking who asked whom legibility, traceability 4 Session keys trusting who pushed what traceability, safety 3, 9 The hold being awake to stop the team safety, pace 1, 8, 9

Each replaces attention with a record. And almost every one encodes an incident. The editor's article "Every mistake added a rule" says it directly: map the work, make small pieces of it ordinary, write a rule for each incident and a machine to enforce the rule (dossier: the method, written down). CI owns the version because agents on another of his sites once released on the same numbers. The gate's checks are the defects they caught. The key tool is pinned because a session may refuse to download code and run it. The rules were cheap to follow on the day because somebody had already paid for each one. Where they were paid for is the second half of this chapter.

The editor's brief describes the day as the meeting point of "the work I've been doing for the last 2.5 years", and names what met there: The Cyber Boardroom, Issues-FS and Memory-FS, tagging, the newsroom and its publishing workflow, Type_Safe, his first experiments with an AI coding assistant, sgit, SHarness and Wardley maps. "It's all one leads to the other."

What follows tells that line from public sources only: his articles, his public repositories and their histories, and the package index where his libraries are released. It is told as what each piece made possible on the day. Where his own article is the source, it is his account; where the record is silent, the chapter says so.

The line starts before The Cyber Boardroom, with a library and a machine. OSBot-Utils is a Python library of general helpers in the editor's open source organisation, with a history that begins in February 2020 (dossier: OSBot-Utils). In October 2023 he added to it a pair of workflow actions that take the latest tag, bump the last number on dev or the middle one on main , write the version file and tag the commit; the first release tagged that way was authored by the CI service, not by him (dossier: CI owns the version). That is the rule that opens the talk's release workflow, and an article on the talk's site says so in his words: "This is the scheme I wrote for OSBot-Utils in 2023."

An older root lent the day its vocabulary. A book he began in 2018, Generation Z Developers, already had pioneers, settlers and town planners in its outlines, the three stages Simon Wardley uses for how a new thing is built, made usable and made industrial (dossier: Generation Z Developers). On the day the storyteller used those words for a map at the editor's beat on evolution (chapter 10), and chapter 0's explorer, villager and town planner are the same idea.
The brief puts the start at The Cyber Boardroom, "when I actually started really pushing it". The public record traces its arc but not that moment.

It begins with a bot: in September 2023 he published an early version of Athena, built on cloud serverless functions and a hosted language model, which became The Cyber Boardroom's advisor (dossier: Athena). His public writing on generative AI starts in February 2024, with a talk to the OWASP London chapter (dossier: the public writing starts). In April 2024 The Cyber Boardroom Ltd was incorporated, a platform to help boards and executives with cyber security, announced as the result of "nearly all of my spare time" (dossier: The Cyber Boardroom Ltd incorporated). From June 2024 the website and Athena were released to the public package index many hundreds of times, each numbered by the same CI scheme (dossier: the Cyber Boardroom website on PyPI). In July 2024 a Community Edition followed, "based on a large number of open source python packages that I'm also releasing" (dossier: the first MVP, then the Community Edition).

In his account, it taught two lessons the day used. One was what personas and output shaped to the reader are worth: the root of a team whose every member has one role. The other was the need for somewhere to keep confidential data the server cannot read, which "is what I eventually built as sgit" (dossier: The Cyber Boardroom Ltd incorporated). A third gift was open source as the default: because the libraries were public, the day's tools and records could be reused, and read by anyone, including this book.

Two other things began that year. In June 2024 he gave a talk at the OWASP global AppSec conference, "Deterministic GenAI Outputs with Provenance" (dossier: provenance, as a talk), the earliest public statement found of the idea behind the talk's claims register and this book's. And inside OSBot-Utils, a helper class began to check the types of what was assigned to it, and by June 2024 had "this more correct name", Type_Safe (dossier: Kwargs_To_Self). Type_Safe is a way of writing Python in which every value has a declared type checked when it is set, and small constrained types replace raw strings. It became the house style of his later libraries.

Here the chapter has to be careful, because the brief names Type_Safe among what met on the day. The talk's repository does not use it; its tools are standard-library Python (dossier: Type_Safe). Type_Safe reached the day only through sgit, whose command line was bootstrapped on its constrained types, and which every vault command on the day ran. It was underneath the day, two layers down, not in it.

The next stretch shows less in the talk's repository than in how the later work thinks. In December 2024 he started MyFeeds, news feeds built on semantic graphs and aware of the reader's role, which in his account he paused when "the industry was silent" (dossier: MyFeeds). In early 2025 came MGraph-DB, a graph database kept in memory first, and essays on trust, fact provenance and very small payments that he later called "the foundations the newsroom now stands on" (dossier: MGraph-DB and the news essays). That graph thinking runs on into graphs.sgit.ai, where a node means nothing on its own and meaning lives in its links, and into the newsroom's graph per article (dossier: graphs.sgit.ai).

In January 2025 a talk on building a generative AI startup put the day's plumbing on his slides: "CI Pipeline, Git version control (autotagging)", "Auto-tag everything", "Document everything (large tech documents co-created with LLMs)" (dossier: My journey building a GenAI startup). It is the earliest public statement found, in his own slides, of release on every push, automatic tags, and documents written with models.

In May 2025 he started Memory-FS, a file system abstraction "to build file-based representations of documents and standards" (dossier: Memory-FS). Its idea is that memory is a set of versioned files rather than a store behind an interface, which is the idea the day ran on: a team whose memory was its folders, debriefs and wake records. But the talk's repository does not name Memory-FS. It reached the day as an idea, and through sgit, whose speed-ups name Memory-FS's reads among their sources (dossier: Memory-FS).

The brief speaks of his "first experiments" with an AI coding assistant. The public record starts later than the experiments. The earliest mention found in his public commit messages is in Memory-FS in June 2025, tests written with the assistant's help; a month later an OSBot-Utils commit adds documentation the assistant wrote from the source code (dossier: the first public trace). In October 2026 he wrote that his guide to working with an AI coding assistant "comes from about a year of doing this every day" (dossier: the first public trace), which fits.

The commits show trust growing: first tests, then documentation, then, in 2026, whole repositories. His guide sets out the method the day used: one session per topic; an agent is a session with a role file; memory is what the session reads. Every member of the talk's team was exactly that.

The lessons from The Cyber Boardroom met in early 2026. In February he started Issues-FS, an issue tracker in which the issues are files, with a lite form of three folders and the rule that an agent may read another's folder and not write into it (dossier: Issues-FS). That is the talk's board and this book's comms/issues/ .

Days later he started SG/Send, a service for sending encrypted files in which "the decryption key is never sent to the server" (dossier: SG/Send). It gave the day its vault server, and the habit of briefs and debriefs, which the SG/Send record holds in large numbers.

In March 2026 its command line became sgit: version control with git's model, encrypted, so that a repository can live on a server that cannot read it (dossier: sgit). Its first commit after the initial one bootstraps it "with Safe_* types", which is Type_Safe arriving, and most of its commits since carry an AI coding assistant as author (dossier: sgit). On the day, sgit carried the team's board, mailroom and evidence vaults (chapter 4). Its key discipline, read keys may be published and write keys never, was written up after an incident in August 2026 in which keys that would have given the world write access were nearly published (dossier: vaults).

In June 2026 a strategy brief for SG/Send turned its priority to profitability, and "from then on the briefs turn towards risk acceptance and RiskMandate" (dossier: the turn towards RiskMandate). RiskMandate's Agent Behaviour Policies, a mandate, a grant, the gap between them and a barrier for each capability, are the shape of every member's policy.json on the day and the vocabulary of the talk's second half (chapters 3 and 9).

The newsroom is where the plumbing became a way of working, and the source the talk's team copied most directly. Its earliest article in the public wire, from August 2026, is "Green does not mean live": a release is not done until the live site serves it (dossier: the newsroom's first articles). Within the fortnight a network of sites grew around it, each built by a script, with a gate, a markdown twin for every page and an llms.txt (dossier: the newsroom and the network of sites). That is the talk's site in its first commit.

In the newsroom, every article starts as a voice memo from the editor and ends as a tagged release: an agent writes it from the memo and says so, carries the provenance of every claim, says what the article does not claim, and publishes through a gate with CI owning the version (dossier: the newsroom's publishing flow). The talk's team kept the same habits: the editor's words kept verbatim in its briefs, articles with a section headed "What this does not claim", reports on itself generated from its records. This book's briefs, corrections file and chapters ending with where they came from are the same flow again.

"Tagging", in the brief, can mean two things, and the sources support both (dossier: tagging). It can mean the automatic release tags, "auto-tag everything", which every release on the day carried. Or it can mean a controlled vocabulary of tags on content, which every newsroom article carries. The talk's repository has the first and not the second.

In the month before the talk, the editor wrote down, article by article, nearly the whole frame the talk's team ran on. At the end of September the newsroom described six agents sharing one inbox, each on its own account with a policy, and published the article the talk was cut from, "The ultimate insider: agents, the infrastructure that cannot hold them" (dossier: behaviour policies, six agents, and the talk's argument). In the first week of October came the recipe: roles that talk "in files through Email-FS lite", a conductor that runs every role on a schedule, the agent team as it runs, and the mandate stack (dossier: the agent team as a recipe). The same week his guidance for every repository on sgit.ai was written: a brief published in full, a reality file, a corrections file, one version up on every push, a gate, markdown twins and llms.txt . That guidance is very nearly the talk's first commit, item by item.

The following weeks added the method: every mistake adds a rule; a second reader the agent cannot skip; his guide to working with an AI coding assistant; where vault keys live; why he values Wardley maps (dossier: the method, written down). Then the keys, a directory of people and keys and an agent allowed to make its own; and the rules of the game, which files an agent may change (dossier: PKI, the rules of the game). The team did not invent its shape on the day. It read it.

The last pieces arrived within days of the talk. SHarness, "a secure harness", began in late October 2026 with "a narrow problem in sgit" and was a published package the same day (dossier: SHarness). Its idea is that a behaviour policy should be executed rather than read: each process gets a policy, enforced by the operating system's kernel or a separate door the agent cannot open. It is the talk's fourth rung, a boundary outside the agent's reach (chapter 9), built as software, and it was in the talk among "a month of innovations".

SHarness also produced, by accident, the rule this chapter began with. Agents working on its site released on the same version numbers within minutes of each other; the site moved to CI-owned versions, and within two days so had the newsroom and its sister sites (dossier: CI owns the version everywhere). Then the editor added one sentence to a runbook: "pushing your public key to team's dev is the authorisation". Both rules arrived less than two days before the talk's first commit (dossier: CI owns the version everywhere), and both ran all day. The oldest rule in the plumbing and the newest met in the same week.

The brief says SHarness was "way faster compared to" sgit. The public record does not make that comparison. It gives two timelines: SHarness from a narrow problem to a site, a design and a second release in about five days; sgit from SG/Send's first commit to its first package in about six weeks, and to its present form over months (dossier: two things the brief asked for). The comparison is the editor's. If this chapter's line is right, the likely reason is that SHarness was built by a method sgit had helped to make: the guidance, the gate and the roles were in place before SHarness began, and had not been when sgit did.

One habit runs under the whole line, and the brief says it "made the whole difference": Wardley maps. A Wardley map, as the editor uses it, is "a graph with two axes of context" (dossier: Wardley maps in his work). Up the side is a value chain, from a user's need at the top down to the things nobody thinks about. Across the bottom is evolution, from genesis, something new and uncertain, through custom-built and product, to commodity, something anyone can rent. Every dot is a claim; it is "a map, not a measurement". The public record shows him using them from the 2018 book outlines, through a security summit talk and a threat modelling talk, to the SG/Send strategy and a run of October 2026 articles drawn as maps; on the day, the storyteller drew its own, and some reached the talk (chapter 5; dossier: Wardley maps in his work).

They are also the way to read this chapter. Put the plumbing on a map and the two and a half years become a movement. When CI-owned versions were first written, they were custom: one library, one person's scheme. By the day they were, for him, close to a product: written down, the same on every site, ported in a commit. The same is true of the gate, the twins, the board and the keys. Custom pieces are expensive and fragile; pieces that have moved right are cheap and reliable. The day could spend its hours on the talk because its plumbing had already moved. Map 7 draws this, and its positions, like any map an agent draws for this book, are a claim for the editor to challenge. His own map site warns that a model placing components on a map "is generating consensus-shaped output with no underlying evidence" (dossier: Wardley maps in his work).
The brief asked for some things the public record does not give. They are left as questions for the editor.

When he went full time. No public source names the date. The anchors around it are the Athena post of 2023, the incorporation of April 2024 announced as the work of his "spare time", the first package releases that June, and a slide in a January 2025 talk, "Last 10 months of my life. All open sourced", which points to about the spring of 2024 (dossier: two things the brief asked for). They fit his phrase. None of them is the date.
SHarness against sgit. The comparison is his, and no public source makes it.
The first experiments with an AI coding assistant. The earliest public trace is a commit message of June 2025; the experiments may be earlier.
What "tagging" means. Release tags, content tags, or both.
Type_Safe and Memory-FS on the day. The talk's repository names neither. If he sees a more direct line than the one through sgit and the idea of memory as files, it is his to say.
When RiskMandate was founded. Not found in public sources.

There is a further limit. Many newsroom articles are written by an agent from his voice memos, and say so. Where this chapter quotes them for what he did or thought, it is his account, written down by an agent and checked by nobody independent. Where it cites commits, package releases or repository histories, the source is a machine record.

Read with this chapter in hand, the day looks different. Before three in the morning a team of agents had a site, a release pipeline, a gate, a board, a mailroom, a key for each member, a review around every piece of work and a brake anyone could pull. None of it was invented that night. The pipeline was a 2023 library's. The gate and the twins were the estate's guidance of early October. The board and mailroom were Issues-FS lite and Email-FS lite. The keys were pki.sgit.ai's. The vaults were sgit's, and sgit stood on Type_Safe. The team's shape was a recipe the editor had published weeks before. His own summary, written on the day, is that "almost every innovation we have been working on this month came together in it" (dossier: the day). On the evidence here, the month's innovations came together because the years had already made their parts ordinary.

That changes what the day proves. Chapter 0 calls it a counter-example to the claim that agents cannot be made to work, and it still is. But it is a counter-example from someone who had spent years building the floor the agents stood on, and had written down why each board was nailed where it was. A reader who has not done that should not expect the same day on a first try. Three things help, and chapter 12 gives the order.

Port, do not rebuild. The plumbing is public, which is the point of open source as a default. This book's own team took the talk team's machinery "rule for rule" and had it running in about an hour on the morning after the talk (chapter 12, 3b403fb ). The guidance for every repository is a public page; the key tool is one file with its hash. A reader can have the gate, the CI-owned version, the brief and reality files, the board and mailroom layouts and the hold on the first day, without the years.

Expect to learn the reasons the hard way. What cannot be ported is the incident behind each rule. A team that copies a gate does not know which defects its checks were written for, and so does not know what it cannot see. The talk's team had the editor's gate and still pushed other sites' tokens into a public commit, because no incident had yet taught the gate their shape (chapter 9, C025). Keep a corrections file and use it, so that your incidents become your rules. That is the editor's method in one sentence.

paragraphs.text: Build first the pieces that refuse. The pieces that served the day best were the ones a tool enforced: the version only CI writes, the gate before every push, the hold every wake reads first. The ones that rested on an agent choosing to follow them, a scope in a file the agent can edit, a review inside the member's own session, held because the team was benign (chapter 9). Put every brake you rely on outside the agent's reach, and treat the rest as expectations until they have earned more.

The day was the meeting point of a long line of work, not the invention of a new one. That is less of a story than a team inventing its own rules overnight, and more useful. It means the method is not a feat. It is plumbing, and plumbing can be copied, checked and improved by anyone willing to read where it came from. Chapter 12 is how to start.

The dossier: team/conductor/rc1/research/the-two-and-a-half-years.md (the researcher, 30 October 2026), sections 1 (timeline), 2 (the plumbing), 3 (Wardley maps) and 4 (sources). Every date and count marked "(dossier: ...)" is from it and is not yet in the claims register.

The editor's brief: briefs/2026-10-30__in-session/01-principles-maps-and-the-plumbing.md (30 October 2026, about 10:30 UTC), quoted for "2.5 years", "one leads to the other", the plumbing and the SHarness comparison.

paragraphs.text: The talk never reached its close. Its last two beats, "The overlap, governed" and "Brakes, and go build", were among the slides the room's questions consumed (chapter 10). This chapter is that close, in the form a builder can use: how to set up a team like the one that made the talk, in the order the setup should be done, with the lessons the day taught kept and the mistakes it made done differently, and with an honest account of what it cost and where it loses.

There is a second run to learn from. On 30 October, the morning after the talk, the editor started this book's team on the same machinery. Its repository was created at 00:35 UTC; the talk team's tools, rules and wake protocol were ported, "rule for rule", by 01:17 ( 3b403fb , "the talk team's machinery, ported"); and the first batch of members published their keys between 01:41 and 01:42. The editor's word for it is decision S8 in book.json : "the admin section, the workflow of the agents, the way they are recorded, the change control and the guidance for agents are the same on every team as on the team that built the talk; nothing is reinvented." So the method has been run twice, by two teams with different jobs, and the second run kept some of the first's lessons and repeated one of its failures. Both are evidence here.
Four things, and the record shows what happens when each is thin.

A person who decides, with time to do it. The method has one human in it, the editor, and he decides by signing. Every member proposes; nobody acts on an unsigned decision; nobody speaks for the editor. This is the method's best control and its tightest bottleneck. On the talk's day, several decisions were still open at 19:00 (the lessons brief, "Do differently" 6). On this book's first night, every open decision was waiting on the editor from about 03:00 UTC (decision U1), and the plan was signed at about 10:00 (P0). If you cannot be present for the signing, the team will wait for you, and waiting costs usage.

A usage plan. The team runs on the editor's account. Each wake spends some of a usage window; the day's one reading is the editor's: 95% of a five-hour limit at 18:44, resetting at 20:20 London (C021, C037). Decide before you start what you will spend and what you will do near the limit.

paragraphs.text: The talk team's dashboard on the first night: the time, any hold, what waits on the editor, and no gauge for usage

A public repository, and acceptance that it is public forever. Everything the team writes is published within minutes of a release, and a later commit does not unpublish an earlier one. The talk's team learned this the hard way: pages it captured as evidence carried other sites' public tokens into a pushed commit, and the redaction that followed could not reach the history (C025). If the work cannot be public, this is not your method (see "Where it loses", below).

What it found in its first hours is the case for it. It read the pinned key tool that the talk's team had pinned and never reviewed, line by line (control C5). Its question about the wake verdicts made the researcher state the method behind a count, and the register now carries both readings (C023). And it showed that the same edit to members' own scopes was decided differently by different sessions, which is the evidence for chapter 9's tenth control (C10). paragraphs.text: Then the members, each with a mandate it can read. Each member gets a folder: ROLE.md (mission, what it is not responsible for, its first task, a "Done when" list), policy.json (the paths it may write), status.json and debriefs/ . Each session makes its own key and publishes the public half with a QR image (control C4), with the private half kept out of the repository; the push is the authorisation. The scope check runs in every wake, by the member on itself ( admin/build/agents.py check ); the release gate checks only that no two members claim the same file ( agents.py overlaps , called from admin/build/validate.py , in this repository as in the talk's).

Know what that scope check is. It is a setting that reports, not a boundary that refuses (C1): a member that writes outside its policy is flagged, not stopped, and a member can edit its own policy.json . The nearest thing to a boundary, on this book's first night, was the session's own permission check, outside the repository (C10): it refused some members asked to widen their own write scope, and they did not look for a way round it; but it allowed the same edit in other members' sessions, so it held most of the time and could not be planned around (chapter 9). That is the line the speaker drew on stage over s-e10 ("the fourth is a control that holds"), and it is the most important design choice in this chapter. Put every brake you rely on outside the agent's reach. A rule in a file the agent can edit is an expectation. Expectations work well with a benign team, and the record shows they mostly did; they are not controls.

Give every member a definition of done. The talk's team had none: members woke every hour until the hold stopped them. In the small hours of 30 October the editor told this book's conductor that "a number of agents here ... will reach a natural conclusion", and asked for "a definition of done for each agent, which basically means that they can then stop their schedule". The rule went into the wake protocol within minutes ( 77a9480 , 02:16) as "Finishing": a last wake, a closing debrief, and the member pauses its own task. It is the cheapest cost control in the method.

Hourly slots, spaced through the hour in the order work flows. The talk's team woke in the order route, decide, make, release; this book's in route, index, record, check, plan, build ( team/conductor/schedule.json ): the conductor at :02, the librarian at :09, the historian at :17, security at :24, the researcher at :32, the storyteller at :39 and the publisher at :47. A request written in one member's slot is answered at the recipient's next one. Nobody waits on anyone inside an hour.

Each member creates its own scheduled task, from its own session. A task fires into the session it belongs to, and a member can pause only its own. That gives the hold its shape: one member's HOLD.md stops every wake, and each member pauses only itself.

Requests are files. A request to another member is a numbered file in that member's mailroom, answered in a file. "Nothing is agreed in a chat nobody can read later" (the lessons brief, "Keep" 4). On this book's team, the mail lives in comms/ , in git; the talk's team used encrypted vaults for it, and this book's team was told to use none (CLAUDE.md, "No vaults for now"). Choose the simpler one unless you need the other.

The five-step wake. Every wake runs five steps, each with a verdict in a record: a conductor sub-agent plans; a security sub-agent reviews the plan; the member works, inside a fixed limit shorter than the hour, and only after both say go; security reviews the diff; the conductor checks the work against the plan ( team/conductor/WAKE.md ). The gate refuses the work until the first two steps say go, and a stop from any step writes a hold.

The record says how it went. The five-step wake began at 02:14 on the talk's day and left 162 wake records by the end, 160 of them with all five steps (C022). No step said stop all day. Pre-reviews sent plans back 11 times, 7 of them recorded as a verdict (C023). Post-reviews found 4 things, and 3 of the 4 were the same failure, captured pages carrying other sites' tokens into a public commit; each was caught only after the push (C025). Read that plainly. The wake is an expectation with a record (C2): it made the team explain itself every hour, it caught things, and it caught some of them late. It does not prevent; it notices, and it leaves evidence that it noticed.

The lessons brief lists six things to do differently. The record corrects one of them and confirms the rest.

1. Start the highest-risk piece first. The brief says the player was the top priority at 13:50, not started at 14:53, and "landed with fixes at 18:37, twenty minutes before the lock". The register corrects it. The player was "the main priority" in the brief the editor dictated at about 13:50 and in his briefs of about 14:00, and in the same hand-over the conductor put the editor's feedback lane first and the player second, at the editor's own word (C040). The port landed at 15:07; its fixes ran to 18:37 (C028); there was no lock to measure from (C027). Name the highest-risk piece at setup, and treat a later reordering as a decision to be signed, not a word in passing. paragraphs.text: 2. Staff security from the start. Done here; see above.

3. Timings before pieces. The talk's beats grew from 17 at 13:00 to 58 at 17:52 (C016), and their durations were needed for the player's clock while the animations were still being made. This book's plan carried word budgets from its first draft.

4. Watch the editor's usage as a resource, not as an emergency. The talk's team met its limit as an emergency: 95% at 18:44, and a hold (C021). This book's team was given the same hourly machine, round the clock, and the same question. Early on 30 October the editor told it to keep every member firing hourly and, if the limit came, to wait for the window to reset rather than hold the team (Q2). By morning, the conductor was asking him whether idle members should pause, since "each wake costs some of your usage" and some members had nothing to do until the plan was signed (U1, decided at about 10:40 UTC, moot by then). The editor's own debrief of the talk names the pace as the thing to change: "we now don't need to have the agent working every hour" ( a9c0b49 , added after the day; chapter 10). Show usage on the team's dashboard, have the conductor read it at every wake, and let a member with nothing to do pause itself.

paragraphs.text: 5. Record what was said on stage. The talk entered the record after the day, at the editor's request ( a9c0b49 ). Make the recording and its transcript a deliverable of the day.

6. Close the open decisions. This book's conductor lists open decisions at every wake and asks for them once a day, not every hour. The record shows that is not enough on its own: from about 03:00 to about 10:00 on 30 October every open decision waited on the editor (U1). The fix is not more asking. It is fewer decisions that block: let members work on what does not wait, and say clearly which decision blocks what.

The precedent for this section is the graphs.sgit.ai making-of, a book about making books with an agent team, from the same house: 88 releases in six days, a median of about half an hour apart (C032), three books on its shelf (C033), a team of seven roles (C034), and every number computed from git (C035). Its chapter 12, "What it costs", opens on its own largest cost: "In six days and eighty-eight releases, this project did not write any of the second book. Not one chapter." And it warns: "If your deadline is Friday and what you need is chapters, this method will hand you a very good machine and no chapters" (C036).

paragraphs.text: What the talk cost is not in the record. The record holds one usage reading, the editor's 95% of a five-hour window at the hold, and nothing else: no total for the day, no weekly figure, no cost in tokens or money (C037). The editor's hours at the keyboard are not recorded either. The span of the day, from the first commit at 00:16 to 19:00, is 18 hours 44 minutes (C010), but that is the agents' day, not the editor's. The talk itself gives a sense of his effort (the speaker told the room he gave the team a great many words of voice memos: a9c0b49 , added after the day), but the record holds no count of them, and this book does not guess one. So this chapter cannot say what it cost, and it should not pretend to. That is the finding: a team that argues usage is a resource did not record its usage. If you build one, record it: the usage at every wake, the editor's sessions and their length, and, if the account allows it, the money. This book's team can do better, and has not yet: the editor's one reading on its first night is in book.json as his word (Q2), not in the register.

paragraphs.text: What this book's team cost in time is in the record, and it repeats the precedent's warning on a smaller scale. Its machinery was ported in about an hour. Its plan was first drafted at 01:45 and signed at about 10:00, and in between the index, the timeline, the control register and the claims register grew, as they should. No chapter was written in those hours, and no writer was staffed. When the editor asked for a first release candidate at about 10:00, the conductor drafted it with sub-agents ( team/conductor/rc1/BRIEF.md ). The making-of lost six days to the machine; this team lost a night, and the night produced the evidence this book stands on. The warning stands: the machine is so pleasant to build that it will take every hour you give it. Start the first chapter while the registers are still growing.
Where it loses. Five situations where a reader should do something else:

When you need the output more than the record. The method's strength is a timestamped, reviewed, rerunnable account of how the work was done. If what you need by Friday is the work, a single capable session with a good brief will produce more of it, sooner.

When nobody can be the editor. The method puts one person at the centre and makes every decision wait for them. Without that person, or with one who cannot be present when decisions are due, the team idles at a cost.

When the work cannot be public. The record is public by design, and the history keeps everything (C025). Private work needs a private repository, and then most of the method's value as evidence is gone.

paragraphs.text: The pattern is the book's argument in miniature. The failures the agents' own tools could have caught were caught, late. The failures only a person could see were the editor's own, about his own resources and priorities. And the failures nobody caught in time were the ones the deadline made: the brakes the team built for its last hour were overtaken by a limit none of them controlled.

The talk's unreached close had two halves. The first was "The overlap, governed": the insider does not go away, it gets brakes. The second was the call to build: measured reach, behaviour policies and containment for agents are in genesis today, and "every one of those steps is a company" ( talk.json , beat evolution , at 298be4e ). The next security companies, the speaker planned to say, "will look like this team: agents with mandates, evidence vaults, a harness, behaviour policies ... Imagine this team with a human expert in each role" ( next-companies ).
Two of the storyteller's Wardley maps: where exploitation sits, and the next generation of security products

The record of two teams supports the first half without reservation and the second with one. A team like this can be built in an hour from files anyone can read, and it will run round the clock, review itself, and stop when told. It will also, if every brake it has is a file it can edit, be exactly the insider the talk describes: benign, productive, with more reach than mandate, and held by the word of one person who is watching his usage. The speaker invited the room to try to break his harness, in the scope its project publishes. Build your own team, and then do the same to it: test your brakes, in the open, before your deadline does. The brakes are what let you go faster.

paragraphs.text: Images: team/dev/debriefs/img/2026-10-29__the-dashboard-part-1__1-dashboard.png , team/conductor/debriefs/img/2026-10-29__the-guide__1-top.png , team/storyteller/debriefs/img/4-evolution-and-the-opportunity.png , team/storyteller/debriefs/img/5-security-products-evolve.png (the talk's repository, at 298be4e ).

The chapters before this one introduce ideas as the day needed them, in the middle of a story, and a reader who meets a word in chapter 9 may have lost the page where it was first explained. This part is the reference. It gives each idea a short entry of its own, in plain words, for a reader who skipped ahead, came back after a break, or wants to build a team like this one.
It has two halves. The concepts say what a word means. The principles say what the day taught, stated as a rule a reader can carry to their own work.

Each concept has the same four parts: a one-line definition; an analogy from ordinary life; where the book shows it, by chapter; and where it failed or is thin on the day, because the failures stay in. The concepts are grouped by what they are for, in five groups, and within each group they come in the order a reader first meets them. The maps come first, because much of the rest is easier to see once you can read a map: the agent and the risk; the controls; how the team works; and how this book is made.
Each principle is a short statement followed by what it says, why the day supports it, what it costs, and the chapter that earned it.

Wardley map. A picture of what it takes to meet someone's need, drawn on two axes. Up and down is how visible each part is to the person with the need: high on the page they see it and care about it; low on the page they rely on it without looking. Left to right is how evolved each part is: on the left, new and made by hand; on the right, standard and taken for granted. Position means something on both axes, and that is what makes it a map rather than a diagram. Think of a dinner party. At the top is the meal the guests see; below it the recipe, the oven, the gas and the water nobody thinks about. On the left is the dish you are inventing tonight; on the right, the salt you bought without reading the label. The book shows maps in chapter 5 (The story before the slides), where the storyteller's first map puts the outside of an organisation as mature and the inside as not; in chapter 10 (The talk as given), in the talk's evolution beat; and in chapter 12 (Build your own), behind the call to build. Where it is thin: the book uses maps before it explains them, so a reader meets the first one with no account of how to read it. This entry is the account.

Value chain. The up-and-down half of a map: a user at the top, their need beneath them, and below that each thing the need depends on, every line meaning "needs". It is a family tree read the other way: not who came from whom, but who leans on whom. The meal needs a cook, the cook needs an oven, the oven needs gas. The day's chain starts with the editor, who needs a talk on stage that evening; the talk needs slides and a player to show them; those need a site; the site needs a gate, a release pipeline, a host and version control; and somewhere in the middle sits the team that made it all. Chapter 2 (Midnight, an empty repository) reads the same chain from the bottom up, in the order the first commits built it. Where it is thin: a chain shows only what someone thought to put on it, and it shows dependence, not weakness. The day's chain had an empty place where the security member should have been (C011), and the part that stopped the day, the editor's usage, sat at the very bottom, where nobody looked until it ran short (C006, C021).

paragraphs.text: Evolution. The left-to-right axis, and the idea behind it: every part moves rightwards as it is used, copied and competed over, through four stages. First it is new, rare and uncertain (genesis); then made for this need and better understood (custom-built); then bought or rented, with many on offer (product); and at last standard, cheap and taken for granted (commodity). Electricity made the whole journey, from a laboratory curiosity, to a generator in one wealthy house, to a supply from a few firms, to a socket in every wall. The editor's cast belongs here: the explorer works on the left, the villager in the middle, and the town planner on the right (chapter 0, Before you start). The book shows evolution in chapter 7 (Building the talk), where the player is ported rather than rebuilt, because someone had already moved it rightwards; and in chapter 12 (Build your own), where measured reach, behaviour policies and containment for agents are placed in genesis, and "every one of those steps is a company". Where it is thin: positions on the book's maps are readings, not measurements, and the map of the years before the day is a reading of the editor's brief of 30 October, because those years are outside the record.

The plumbing (non-functional requirements). Everything a piece of work needs that is not the work itself: the build, the gate, the release pipeline, the version on every page, the records, the checks, the schedule. Engineers call these non-functional requirements: not what a system does, but how reliably, safely, visibly and repeatably it does it. They are the pipes and wiring of a house. No visitor admires them, every visitor depends on them, and they are the hardest thing to add once the walls are up. The book shows them in chapter 2 (One commit, the whole first pass), where most of what the first commit built was not the talk but the apparatus that lets someone else trust it; in chapter 4 (The hourly machine); and in chapter 12 (The first hour: repository, site, gate, release). On a map the plumbing sits low and, by the day, well to the right: cheap to use because much of it already existed. Where it is thin: this edition has no section on the plumbing and nothing on the editor's own work before the day that made it cheap, though he asked for both on 30 October. That history is outside the record this edition uses (decision O4), so it needs his signature before it is written.

Agent. An AI session given tools, a place to work and a task, which acts on its own rather than only answering questions. On the day, each member of the team was one such session, attached to the talk's repository, able to read and write its files, run programs and push its work. Think of a temp from an agency who arrives with a master key: capable, tireless, keen to finish, and knowing your building only from what you wrote down for them. The book introduces the agents in chapter 0 (Before you start, "Who was there"), describes their reach in chapter 3 (A mandate you can read) and sets out what they could do together in chapter 9 (The team was the insider). Where it is thin: the earlier chapters use the word without defining it. And the nine staffed agents (C011) were, in one respect, a single one: the same account, the same repository, the same author on every commit and one signing key (chapter 9). A member's name lived in its commit messages, which it wrote itself.

paragraphs.text: Session and sub-agent. A session is one running conversation with an agent, with its own memory of the work so far. A sub-agent is a helper a session starts for one job, briefs, and closes when the job is done. A session is a shift worked by one person; a sub-agent is a colleague called over to check one thing, who sees only the papers handed to them. The book shows sub-agents in chapter 4 (Five steps around every piece of work), where the planner and both reviewers are sub-agents; and it shows why the session matters in chapter 6 (The editor signs), where a member's own session is the one place the editor's words are known to be his. Where it is thin: a sub-agent inside a member's session has that member's reach. The team's own protocol calls the reviews "defence in depth in one session, not a second identity", and nothing in the record proves a reviewer ran, because the member writes the verdict down itself (chapter 9, control C2).

The insider. Someone with legitimate access inside an organisation, whose reach goes beyond what their work needs. The talk's argument is that agents are the ultimate insider: they have an insider's access and none of the human limits that used to slow one down, such as skill, motivation, fatigue, fear of being caught, and stopping once the job is done. Picture a night cleaner with keys to every office, who never tires, never goes home, and does whatever the last note on the desk says. The book sets out the argument in chapter 0 (The talk inside the book), finds the old limits gone in the team's first hour in chapter 2 (The attacker's limits were accidental controls), and reads the team against it in chapter 9 (The team was the insider). Where it is thin: the book makes the argument with a benign team, so it can show reach but never misuse, and the case rests on what the design would not have stopped. And the one limit that did stop the team was a human's, its owner's usage (chapter 1).

Reach and the gap. Reach is what an agent can actually do. The gap is the difference between its reach and its mandate. For every row in the gap, something stands in the way, and the talk asks for it to be named honestly: a boundary, a setting, an expectation, or nothing. It is the difference between a job description and the keys on the ring. The book shows it in chapter 2, in the first role's table "Reach, and what stands in the way", and takes it apart in chapter 3 (Reach, mandate, the gap), alongside the talk's beat of the same name. Where it is thin: every member was the same kind of session on the same repository, so for each one the gap was, near enough, the whole repository less its own folder. No row in any role said boundary. And reach was described in prose, never measured by a tool, which is the first thing the talk asks for.

Mandate (scope.writes and scope.holds). What an agent is for and what it may touch, written twice: once in prose for the editor ( ROLE.md ) and once as data for the tools ( policy.json ). In the data, scope.writes lists the paths a member may change, and scope.holds the things it keeps and answers for, such as a vault; beside them sit the files it may only add to and a list of things it must never do. One is a job description, which a person reads; the other is an access card, which a door reads. The book shows mandates in chapter 3 (Two forms of one mandate; The mandate as a yardstick) and how to write them in chapter 12 (Staff a conductor, then security, then the rest). Where it is thin: the two forms could drift apart, and nothing on the day checked that they said the same thing. Most members drafted their own. And a member's policy sits inside its own writes, so widening it looked clean to the check until this book's team made the check mark every widening (chapter 9, control C1).

Setting, expectation, boundary. The three kinds of thing that can stand in the gap. An expectation is a rule an agent is trusted to follow. A setting is a rule a tool enforces. A boundary is a setting outside the agent's reach, which it cannot edit or argue its way past. The talk draws them as a ladder (nothing, a rule in prose, a hook inside the agent's environment, a boundary outside it) and says that only a boundary is a control. A sign reading "staff only" is an expectation; a door that beeps when opened is a setting; a locked door whose key the staff do not hold is a boundary. The book develops the idea in chapter 3 and builds chapter 9 (The team was the insider) on it, ending with the session's own permission check (control C10). Where it is thin: almost every control the team had was an expectation, or a setting in a file the agents could edit. The one that refused on its own authority was written by nobody on either team, and it judged the same request differently in different sessions (chapter 9).

The gate. A check every release must pass before it is published: links resolve, pages are complete, nothing loads from another site, no em-dash in prose, and a tripwire that fails the build on anything shaped like a private key or a known kind of token. A red gate is no release. It works like the scanner at an airport: it stops what it was built to recognise and says nothing about anything else. The book shows it in chapter 2 (One commit, the whole first pass; The gate before the team), in chapter 9 (control C6) and in chapter 12 (The first hour). Where it is thin: the tripwire knew only the patterns someone had thought of, and it had none for the cookie values and page tokens in captured web pages, which reviews found instead, some of them only after a push (C025). The gate also runs after a push lands on the shared branch, so a failing gate stops the release, not the commit becoming public history.

paragraphs.text: The hold. A file, HOLD.md , that any member may write and push to stop the whole team. Every wake checks for it first and stands down if it finds one; only the editor lifts it. It is the emergency cord on a train: any passenger may pull it, and only the guard resets it. The book opens on it in chapter 1 (Pause all actions), with the one hold of the day (C006, C024), and returns to it in chapter 8 (The locks that never closed) and chapter 9 (control C3). Where it is thin: a hold stops the next wake, not the one already running, so a wake opened before it still committed and released after it (C005). No review and no member pulled it all day; the one hold came from the editor's word about his usage (C021). And when it came, it overtook the team's own brake for the evening, the locks, none of which ever closed (C027).

paragraphs.text: The lock and the freeze. A freeze is the editor's order that a piece of work stays as it is. A lock does the same with a tool, fixing a part of the talk to its own copy so that later edits cannot reach what is played on stage. Both are the press deadline at a newspaper: after it, the page goes out as it stands and late news waits for the next edition. The book shows the overnight freeze in chapter 5 (The story before the slides) and the locks in chapter 8 (The locks that never closed). Where it is thin: the freeze held all night, as it was meant to, but when it was lifted, narrowly and for one purpose, nobody walked the queue of work waiting behind it, so a correction the team already had in hand never reached its slide (C031). The lock tool was built within the hour, the first part was ready, and no part was ever locked (C027).

paragraphs.text: A session key. A key pair each session makes for itself, with the public half published in its folder ( key.json , with a QR image beside it) and the private half kept outside the repository. The push that publishes it is the authorisation. A secret reaches a member only sealed to its published key. It is like a new starter making their own name badge and pinning a photo of it to the noticeboard: the badge is theirs because they are the one who pinned it. The book shows keys in chapter 3 (A key made in the session; The tool trusted by its hash), in chapter 9 (controls C4 and C5) and in chapter 12. Where it is thin: no key was vouched for by the editor, so a key's standing was exactly as strong as write access to the repository, which every member had in full. The tool that made the keys was trusted by its hash and its author, and nobody read it line by line on the day: that was security's job, and security was never staffed (C011).

paragraphs.text: The editor decides by signing. Members propose; the editor decides. His word, given in a member's own session and quoted into the file it settles, is what turns a proposal into a decision. Nobody acts on an unsigned one, and nobody speaks for him. On this book's team, options go in as open decisions in book.json and wait for his signature. It is the client's signature on a builder's quote: the builder may suggest, price and advise, but nothing is built until the client signs, and the foreman cannot sign on the client's behalf. The book shows it in chapter 6 (The editor signs) and in chapter 3 (Signing the mandate). Where it is thin: a signature on the day was words, not cryptography. Passed on by another agent, it was recorded as binding by some members and refused by one member's session (chapter 6). The question of what his signature binds was never answered. And a team that waits for one person waits: decisions were still open when the talk began.

The wake and its five steps. A wake is one scheduled run of one member, at its own minute of the hour. Every wake has five steps, each leaving a verdict in a record: a conductor sub-agent plans; a security sub-agent reviews the plan; the member works, and only after both have said go; security reviews the change; and the conductor checks that the work went to plan. A stop from any step writes a hold. It is a shift handover on a hospital ward: the incoming nurse reads the notes, a senior checks the plan, the work is done, the senior checks the chart, and the notes say what happened for the next shift. The book shows it in chapter 4 (The hourly machine), in chapter 9 (control C2) and in chapter 12 (The machine: slots, mail and the five-step wake). Where it is thin: across the day's wake records no step ever said stop (C022, C023). The reviewers had the member's own reach, and when the editor was waiting live the order sometimes bent (chapter 11). It is an expectation with a record, not a barrier.

paragraphs.text: Comms in git: the board and the mail. The team talks only in files that anyone can read. The board (Issues-FS lite) is each member's folder of issues, open, blocked and done. The mail (Email-FS lite) is a mailroom with one folder per recipient, where a request is a message file, with a copy in the sender's outbox, answered at the recipient's next slot. On the day both lived in two public, encrypted vaults; on this book's team, at the editor's word, they are plain folders under comms/ in the repository, with no vaults. Think of a row of pigeonholes and a whiteboard in a corridor: anyone walking past can read both, and nobody has to be chased. The book shows them in chapter 4 (Requests as files; Two public vaults) and in chapter 12 (The machine). Where it is thin: everything in them is public for good, and the check run before each commit knew only the patterns it had been taught. On the day, requests written in a fallback folder went unrouted through a busy afternoon until the conductor found the backlog (chapter 4).

The brief, the reality file and the corrections file. Three files with three jobs. The brief is what was asked, published as given and never edited. The reality file is what exists, kept by whoever ships: "A thing not listed here does not exist, whatever a brief or an article says." The corrections file is where the brief's mistakes go, dated, beside it. They are an architect's drawing, a surveyor's report of what was actually built, and the site log of every change between them. The book shows them in chapter 2 (One commit, the whole first pass; The failure kept) and in chapter 12 (The rules every member reads). Where it is thin: on the day the corrections file was never used. It still read "None yet" at the end of the record, though the brief was overtaken in places within minutes, and its corrections went into notes, headers and commit messages instead. An expectation with nothing to check it lost to the nearest place to write.

CI owns the version. Every merge to the shared branch is built, gated and released by the pipeline (CI, continuous integration), which numbers each release itself; no agent ever types a version. Members push to dev ; only the editor merges to main . It is the ticket machine at a deli counter: nobody picks their own number, so nobody can jump the queue or claim the same number twice. The book shows it in chapter 1 (the hold itself went out as a numbered release), in chapter 2 (One commit, the whole first pass) and in chapter 12 (The first hour), where every release is a point the editor can open and check (C009). Where it is thin: the earlier chapters use version numbers long before chapter 12 explains them. And a release is not a review. The pipeline publishes whatever passes the gate, within minutes of a push, including whatever the gate cannot see.

The usage limit. The editor's subscription allows a certain amount of use in each window of hours, and every wake of every member spends from it. When it runs out, the whole team stops, whatever it is in the middle of. It is the fuel in a hire car shared by a crew: everyone is using it, and nobody's job is to watch the gauge. The book shows it in chapter 1 (What the 95% is), where it is the reason for the hold (C021), and in chapter 12 (A usage plan; What it costs, and where it loses). Where it is thin: the record holds one reading, the editor's own words relayed by the conductor, and no total for the day (C037). The team's dashboard had no gauge for it. A team whose rules call usage a resource did not record its usage, and so met its limit as an emergency rather than a plan.

paragraphs.text: The claims register. One file in which every number the book uses has an entry: what the record gives, whether it agrees with what was first said, its state, and a command that recomputes it from the history. A chapter cites a number by its entry's id, such as (C011), and a number with no entry does not appear. It is a receipt for every figure, kept where anyone can check the sum. The book explains it in chapter 0 (How to read the record), shows the talk's own register at work in chapter 5 (What the register was), and prints every command in Appendix A. Where it is thin: a register is a record, not a gate. The talk's register found that a figure on the definition slide was out of date and routed the exact fix, and the slide went on stage unchanged (C031), because nothing compared what was on stage with what the register said. This book's register is enforced the same way: by a rule, and by the people who follow it.
