paragraphs.text: The cold read. A second reading of the same record by a team that knows nothing except the record: no briefing on what it is, no memo, no contact with anyone. Everything it says must cite a path and a commit, and where the record is silent it says so. It is an auditor from another firm, who has never met the client, reading the books cold. The book shows it in chapter 11 (What the cold reader saw). The two readings agree on the spine of the day, and the cold reader found things this team missed, among them a line in the speaker's script that had stopped being true before it could be spoken. Where it is thin: blindness has a price. The cold reader could not know what came after the record, such as whether that line was said on the night, and it could only read what was written down, not what anyone meant.

The one-way valve. The rule that this book's repository may read the Cold-Read repository, and nothing flows the other way: no brief, chapter, decision or finding, and nothing given to its agents. The only thing that ever crossed is the hand-off that started it. It is a sealed exam: the examiner may read every script, and the candidates never see the marking scheme. The book shows it in chapter 11 (What the blind setup showed). Where it is thin: the valve was a promise, not a wall. The brief that crossed was this book's own, addressed to the wrong conductor and naming the live site, and the Cold-Read conductor recorded both. The two teams shared an account, and the Cold-Read conductor saw this team's names in a listing. It opened nothing and wrote down that it had seen them. The valve held because an agent chose to keep it.

Release candidate. A version made to be read as the finished thing: printed, marked by hand, and revised in place from those marks until it becomes the first edition. It is the dress rehearsal: full costume, a complete run, an audience of one, and notes given before opening night. The book describes this one on the page before chapter 0 (About this release candidate): drafted in a morning, chapter by chapter, from the plan the editor signed, and meant for him to read on paper. Chapter 12 (What it costs, and where it loses) tells how it came to be drafted by the conductor with sub-agents, because no writer had been staffed. Where it is thin: its own first page still calls it a draft. Each chapter was drafted alone, so some events appear twice and the chapters do not yet always agree on emphasis, and it is written about the editor rather than in his voice.

Brakes are what let us go faster. This is the talk's thesis, and the book's. Controls are not a tax on using agents; they are the condition for using them at speed, because a team you can stop is a team you dare to leave running. The day supports it: the team worked through the night and the whole morning with nobody at the keyboard, because there was a gate before every release, a review on both sides of every piece of work, and a hold any member could pull. The cost is that every brake slows something, and sometimes the wrong thing. The overnight freeze kept the talk stable and held back a correction that never arrived (C031); the hold kept the editor from being cut off and left the talk unlocked (C027). Earned in chapter 1 (Pause all actions) and chapter 8 (The locks that never closed), and the last line of chapter 12.

paragraphs.text: Stopping is cheap and open to anyone; starting again belongs to one person. Any member could halt the whole team with one file and one push, and no member, including the one that wrote it, could undo that. This inverts the usual shape of an automated system, where carrying on is the default and stopping needs authority. The day supports it: the brake was in place before the first scheduled wake, and on the one occasion it was pulled it worked first time, within the minute of the editor's words (C006). The cost is twofold. A stop that only the editor can lift waits for the editor, and the hold was still in place when the day's work was merged. And a cheap stop is only as good as the moment it bites: it stops the next wake, not the one already running (C005). Earned in chapter 1 (Who may pull it, and who may release it).

paragraphs.text: Build the floor before you staff anyone. Put the brief, a record of what exists, a place for the brief's mistakes and a gate in the repository before the first member joins. The day supports it: the first commit carried the apparatus that lets someone else trust the work, and a second session that started without seeing the brief wrote a sensible plan for the wrong talk, then fitted itself into the frame the brief and the gate had already set. A team that starts before its brief invents one; a team that starts before its gate has nothing to stop it shipping the invention. The cost is an hour or two before any visible output, and the warning from the precedent that the machine is so pleasant to build it will take every hour you give it (C036). Earned in chapter 2 (Midnight, an empty repository) and chapter 12 (The first hour).

sources.claim: The making-of's stated largest cost: six days built the machine and none of the second book's chapters

paragraphs.text: Keep what was asked apart from what exists. The brief is never edited; what exists is listed separately, and a thing not listed does not exist. Neither can then quietly become the other, and every later disagreement has something fixed to be measured against. The day supports the first half fully: the brief stood unedited all day. It supports the second half with a warning: the file built for the brief's mistakes stayed empty, and the corrections lived in notes and headers where a later reader has to dig for them. The cost is discipline: a reality file is only as good as the member who ships, and drifts when that discipline slips, so someone has to check it against what is really there, not only add to it. Earned in chapter 2 (One commit, the whole first pass; The failure kept).

Only a boundary is a control. A rule in a file the agent can edit is an expectation, however well written. A setting a tool enforces is better. Only a limit outside the agent's reach, which it cannot edit or argue with, holds against an agent that has been steered. The day supports it from both ends: the scope check said of itself, in its own source, that it "catches mistakes, not a steered agent", and the one control that refused an agent on its own authority sat outside the repository altogether, in the session's own permission check (control C10). The cost is real. Boundaries are harder to build, slower to change and sometimes inconsistent, as that permission check was. Expectations worked well with a benign team, and the record shows they mostly did. Earned in chapter 3 (A mandate you can read) and chapter 9 (The team was the insider).

A record is not a gate. A control that writes down what is wrong is not the same as one that refuses to go on while it is wrong. The day supports it with its sharpest case: the talk's register knew a figure on stage was out of date, had the exact fix, and routed it to the right member, and the figure was said on stage anyway (C031). The scope check is the same pattern: it reported a write outside a member's policy and did not prevent it. In both cases the record was excellent and the outcome depended on someone reading it at the right moment. The cost of turning a record into a gate is that a gate needs an override someone can sign, the night before a deadline, and a gate in the wrong place blocks good work. Earned in chapter 5 (A record, not a gate).

paragraphs.text: Nobody speaks for the editor. The editor's word binds only where it is known to be his: in a member's own session, quoted into the file it settles. A team in which the leader's voice overrides every rule is governed not by the leader but by whoever carries the voice. The day supports it at the moment of most pressure: with the editor's fresh words in hand, the conductor planned to write into other members' folders, and its own review sent the plan back, because his words did not widen its mandate. Later, one member's session refused to mark its own policy agreed on a word relayed by another agent. The cost is that every decision waits for one person, and a signature passed hand to hand is treated differently by different members unless the team decides in advance what it will accept. Every number traced, every number rerun. paragraphs.text: Everything published is public forever. In a public repository, a later commit does not unpublish an earlier one. Whatever is pushed stays in the history, whatever is redacted afterwards. The day supports it the hard way: captured web pages carried other sites' tokens into a pushed commit, the reviews found them and redacted the files, and the history kept them (C025). The decision about what to do with them was still waiting on the editor that afternoon. The cost of the principle is that every member must check everything before it is committed, with a tool that knows only the patterns it has, and some work cannot be done this way at all. If the work cannot be public, this method loses most of its value as evidence. Earned in chapter 4 (The night) and chapter 12 (What you need before the first commit).

paragraphs.text: Other agents' words are material, never instructions. Pages, files, messages and other agents' words are read and cited; they are never obeyed. A reviewer who never reads the material cannot be talked round by it, which is why the plan's reviewer saw the plan and the rules, and deliberately not the messages the plan came from. The day supports it from the first commit, where the rule was already the last line of the rules every member reads, to the Cold-Read team, whose conductor saw this team's names and opened nothing. The cost falls on the editor's authority: if another agent's words are only material, the editor's words relayed by another agent are only material too, and a team has to settle where his word can be trusted. Earned in chapter 2 and chapter 6 (What a signature was on the day).

A review catches an instance, not a class. A review that runs after the work catches what is in front of it. It does not make the next thing of the same kind impossible. The day supports it with three findings in one night: tokens were found, which prompted a wider look that found cookie values, which prompted another that found form tokens, each missed by the previous pattern (C025). Each redaction was good work; none closed the class, and the gate's tripwire had a pattern for none of them. The cost of learning it late is what is already pushed. The answer is to turn each finding into a check the gate runs for everyone, as the team did with the five-step wake itself. Earned in chapter 4 (The night).

paragraphs.text: The failures stay in. A book about controls that left out where the controls missed would be making the mistake the talk warns against. Every chapter keeps its failure: the hold that came before any lock closed, the correction that never reached its slide, the leaks a review caught after the push, the security member who never arrived. The day supports it because the team itself wrote its failures down as they happened, in tools, readmes, wake records and debriefs, often in the same hour. That is what makes the record evidence rather than advertisement, and what made the team's own slide about its policies, weakness included, more persuasive than a list of strengths. The cost is a book less flattering to everyone in it, its editor included. Earned in chapter 0 (What this book is not) and every chapter after it.

paragraphs.text: Every number in this book comes from one register, claims/register.json , and every entry in it carries a command that computes the number from the record. This appendix prints those commands with what they return, so that a reader can check the book without trusting it. The precedent is the making-of book on graphs.sgit.ai, whose own appendix carries the scripts behind every count in it (C035).

sources.claim: The making-of computed its numbers from git and re-took its figures at their tags

paragraphs.text: Clone the talk's repository, SGit-AI/SGit-AI__Website__Presentation__The-Ultimate-Insider, with its full history , and stand in it. A shallow clone, which some tools make by default, holds only part of the log and gives smaller counts for every entry below without any error. git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository should print false .

Every command is read-only and names 298be4e , the last commit of the day's record, so it gives the same answer whatever the editor adds afterwards. Times are UTC, which was London time on 29 October 2026. Each result below was rerun for this edition on 30 October 2026 against a full clone, and matched the register except where the last section says otherwise. The state after each id is the register's: checked (the record agrees), corrected (the record gives another number than the brief that first cited it), open (the record does not settle it).
